title: A welcome before you walk through the door.
summary: A toy-shop sign in Bath, England, offers something wonderfully practical: quieter music, softer lights and room to be yourself. A note on making welcome specific.
search: My Small World · Bath, EnglandA welcome before you walk through the door.A little toy-shop sign, a place built around play, and a useful idea to bring home to our own Main Streets.An AUsome Life · October 8, 2026An imagined toy-shop welcome, inspired by the story. Original editorial illustration. A photograph of a sign outside My Small World, a toy shop in Bath, England, caught my eye. It announces that the shop is autism friendly. Then it gets to the part I especially like: what that means when you actually arrive. The sign offers to lower the music, soften the lighting and give people space. It reassures visitors about excited play, noise and moments of overwhelm. It invites families to say what would help. “Give you space to be you.”From My Small World’s welcome sign That is a lovely thing to encounter before you have even opened the door. The shop behind the signA whole little world of play. My Small World is an independent toy shop in Bath’s SouthGate shopping area. In the shop’s own account of its beginnings, the idea grew from a search for a special first-birthday present in 2003. That very personal starting point feels fitting for a business whose welcome has travelled so far beyond its front door. The team describes a shop with trees, changing seasonal foliage, birdsong and shelves of books, games, toys and things to make. Play is encouraged. The pleasure of looking, touching and discovering something is part of the visit they want to offer. There is a more recent chapter, too. Revo named My Small World its 2025 Independent Operator of the Year. The award’s description highlights the newer SouthGate store, its playful interior and a sensory space for neurodivergent families. That recognition helps put the much-shared sign in context: the welcome is part of a wider approach to the shop. The relief is in the details. When an ordinary errand takes planning, a specific welcome gives you something to work with. You can picture asking for the music to come down. You know that needing a little room is something the staff have already considered. One less conversation has to begin with an explanation. On its own website, My Small World explains that its team includes autistic people and parents of autistic children. The shop describes a commitment to helping families feel comfortable, grounded in that lived experience. What stays with me is the invitation to arrive as you are. There is room in that idea for a wonderful browse, a very brief visit, a pause, or deciding to try another day. Why it stays with usRoom for the day you are having. A toy shop can hold so much promise: something to turn over in your hands, a favorite subject on a bookshelf, the pleasure of choosing. For a family like ours, that invitation also needs room for an older child, an iPad used for communication and a visit that might be shorter than expected. The particular kindness of the sign is that the adjustments are offered before anyone has to ask. It makes room for a conversation about what would help today. A person can enjoy a lively display and still want the music lowered; someone else may prefer a quiet corner or a little more time. Familiar things within reach. Original editorial illustration. Bring that welcome to our own Main Streets. A bookshop, café, farm stand or hotel can make its welcome useful in the same way: tell people what help is actually available, and make it easy to ask. A few places to begin: Be specific about sound and light. Say whether music can be lowered, which areas are quieter, and what lighting can be adjusted. Offer time and space. Explain where someone can pause and whether they can step outside and return. Ask what helps before stepping in. Welcome different ways of communicating. Give people time to point, type, use picture cards or speak through an AAC device. Address the person directly and respect their answer. Keep the welcome age respectful. Autistic teenagers and adults belong in the picture, too. Offer help without assuming someone’s interests, abilities or preferred language. Those are ideas for other businesses to consider, beyond the adjustments described on this particular sign. The best version is a promise the staff understand and can keep.It can be as ordinary as telling a visitor, “We can lower the music. Would that help?” Then listening to the answer. A welcome has room for “yes,” “no,” “later,” and an answer given without speech. A small sign can start a conversation. For our family, the practical details belong right alongside the lovely ones. The invitation to look around matters. So does knowing that asking for a change will be met with understanding. I would love to see more of that on our own Main Streets: a clear, ordinary welcome, with enough detail to make walking through the door feel a little easier. If Bath is on your listStart with SouthGate’s current shop listing and My Small World’s contact page. The listings give different street numbers following the shop’s move, so confirm the entrance before setting out. The shop’s published telephone number is +44 (0)1225 312943.Ask what can be adjusted during your visit, how the sensory space works and whether there is a quieter time to come. Check the route into the shop, space to move around and nearby accessible toilets separately. A welcoming sign is helpful; each family will still have its own practical questions. About this noteThis is a reflection on a sign spotted online and the shop’s published approach, rather than a report from a family visit. The sign has circulated for years; we are sharing the idea, not announcing a new policy.Read My Small World’s story and autism-friendly approach or contact the shop before a visit. Shop information and the linked Revo award announcement checked October 8, 2026. Ask directly about the adjustments and access details that matter to you. title: October ice cream at Dairy Joy.

October gets apples, pumpkins, and quite a lot of attention for its leaves. We would like to keep ice cream in the conversation.Our stop at Dairy Joy in Weston was a little October outing with James, Mom-Mom and Grandpa Steve—Grandma and Grandpa—and Ruby. Ice cream and time together: a perfectly good reason to get out of the house.Then there was the photo cutout. James had both hands around the top of an enormous painted soft-serve cone, his face in the middle of the swirl, and a grin that made the photograph an immediate keeper. Sprinkles overhead. A bright red lobster alongside. Subtle it was not, and I’m very glad. A little time at the table: Grandpa Steve, James, and Ruby. A table for the afternoon we had.The other photograph is quieter: Grandpa Steve in his blue cap, James in shorts, Ruby beside the bench. Cups on the red tabletop, the tablet in its blue case, sunshine across the stone patio. All the ordinary things that come along with us, right there in the picture.That is what I want to keep from this outing. Not a complicated itinerary or a list of things accomplished. Just family gathered around a table while there was still an October afternoon to enjoy.Summer had officially moved on. We were still finding uses for a picnic table. One more for the family album. title: The furniture store with a fountain show. And cookies.
summary: A real family outing to Jordan’s Furniture in Reading, Massachusetts: Fuddruckers, illuminated fountains, Cookie Monstah and practical access notes.
search: Out & about · Reading, MassachusettsThe furniture store with a fountain show. And cookies.Fuddruckers, Jordan’s Furniture and Cookie Monstah: an afternoon with James in a place that turns out to be considerably more than a furniture store.A family field note · October 2026 · Reading, Massachusetts Lunch first. James at Fuddruckers in Reading, from our family camera roll. Some outings are planned in advance with tickets, schedules and an amount of preparation that could qualify as a second job. And then there is Jordan’s Furniture in Reading, where you can have lunch, watch illuminated fountains, browse a leather sofa and finish with cookies without getting back into the car. We began at Fuddruckers. There’s James in his navy shirt, sitting by the brick wall with that little smile I’m glad I caught. Sometimes the best photograph from a family outing is not in front of the attraction at all. It is the moment everyone has found a place to sit. For food decisions, we had a simple two-picture choice board showing grilled cheese with fries and macaroni and cheese with fries. The board is our own communication aid—not a claim that either dish is on the restaurant’s current menu. Having a familiar way to show a preference matters more to us than any elaborate printed menu. Fuddruckers also had a hand-spun milkshake board, with flavors from chocolate and vanilla to cookies and cream. No one needs to choose a shake to make lunch count, but the menu certainly made a good case for dessert. Our food-choice visual. It is a personal planning tool, not a verified restaurant menu.A little temptation on the Fuddruckers milkshake board. Prices and availability can change. And then the water began to dance.Jordan’s has a water-and-light display known as Liquid Fireworks. In our photographs, water arcs into the dark while green and violet light washes across the room. James is sitting nearby with a big tub of popcorn, looking toward the show.The photographs are some of my favorites from the afternoon. There was something pleasingly old-fashioned about it: a fountain show, a snack, the changing colors and time to watch as long as we wanted. Liquid Fireworks in Reading. Popcorn, fountains and an unexpectedly good stop. A family outing does not become better simply because you managed to fit in six more things. We did pause over the furniture, naturally. There was a beautiful tan leather sectional with a dark wood armrest and a clearance sign. If you find yourself comparing sofas halfway through a water show, that is simply the sort of place Jordan’s is. Cookie Monstah is also inside this same Reading location, so there’s a very appealing cookie-and-ice-cream stop to add if everyone still wants one. The shop is known for fresh-baked cookies and ice-cream cookie sandwiches. I like that this can be part of the afternoon rather than another drive, another parking lot and another set of transitions. We don’t need every part of a place to be suitable for us. The IMAX theater and ropes course are there for people who want them; the food, furniture and water display make a perfectly good smaller outing of their own. A close-up from the fountain show, with the popcorn firmly part of the experience.Yes, there was furniture, too. The very practical side of an otherwise surprising outing. The practical partA simple plan for another family.All three stops are at 50 Walkers Brook Drive, Reading, MA 01867. You can make this a short visit or stretch it out, and you can decide on dessert after you know how the first part of the day is going. 1. Start with lunch.Use the Fuddruckers menu to plan the meal. If visual choices or AAC are helpful, bring familiar pictures, and check the actual options before offering the choice.2. Watch the fountains.Find a position that gives everyone a view without needing to stay close to the sound and colored lights. Popcorn is optional. So is watching the whole show.3. Leave dessert open.Cookie Monstah is right in the complex. A cookie, an ice-cream sandwich—or simply heading home—can all be perfectly good endings. Before you goAccess, sound and the easy exit.MobilityA welcome practical detail from our visit: Jordan’s had wheelchairs available right by the entrance if you needed one. If you plan to borrow one, it is worth checking availability with the store before coming. Fuddruckers’ official Reading page lists wheelchair accessibility. Jordan’s IMAX information lists wheelchair spaces with companion seating, with an assisted entry route on request. Those theater details do not verify every route or attraction elsewhere in the building, so call ahead for individual access requirements.Sound & lightThe water-and-light display includes colored lighting and music, and the surrounding complex can be busy. Choose a viewing distance, bring preferred hearing protection if useful, and keep the option of stepping away. This is not an independently audited sensory-friendly venue.Food & communicationCheck up-to-date menus and allergen information directly. Familiar foods, visual options, AAC, a favorite snack or a short lunch can all help make an outing workable. Do not rely on our photograph of a temporary menu or posted price. title: Thirty-nine minutes of AUsome.
summary: A 39-minute Massachusetts RMV wait becomes a dance party. A mother remembers a security guard, her son James, and connection with very few words.
search: A reflection & photo essayThirty-nine minutes of AUsome.A security guard, my son, and a dance party at the Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles.An AUsome Life · A remembered moment at the Massachusetts RMV 01The RMV, of all places. One of my favorite memories of James happened at the Massachusetts RMV.We waited 39 minutes. And for that entire wait, a security guard kept my son company, entertained him, and showed him the kind of warmth that stays with a mother long after an errand is over.There was an impromptu dance party. Right there. At the Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles.The usual seriousness of the place could wait.I can’t remember whether there was actual music. Some RMV Muzak drifting through the room, maybe. A cell phone playing somewhere. Or perhaps they were dancing to some shared, unspoken groove.And does it even matter?I remember the two of them. Whatever the music was, or wasn’t, they had found each other. 02An arm lifted. An answer. 03The conversation keeps going. I love looking at these photographs. James in his red shorts and blue shoes. The guard in his uniform, his badge still hanging at his waist. The tiled floor. The waiting-room chairs. The signs telling everybody where to go and what to have ready.And in the middle of all that ordinary, official business: these two.An arm goes up. Another follows. They turn toward each other. The next movement becomes another invitation, another response. James is right there in the exchange, bringing his own movement and attention to it.Few words passed between them. Yet watching them, I felt that everything that mattered in that moment was being communicated. There was a whole conversation happening on that tiled floor. 04Two people making something together. 05A waiting room with room for joy. The world isn’t always this AUsome. I wish it were.A family can love its life deeply and still need the world to do better by it. I know both of those feelings. I can treasure this memory and still wish that being welcomed so wholeheartedly felt more ordinary.In a life shaped in part by profound autism, so much thought goes into helping other people understand what James needs. Then someone comes along who takes an interest in him, finds a way to connect, and keeps showing up in that connection. For the length of a wait. For the length of a dance.Those people become part of our family’s story.This man gave James his attention throughout those 39 minutes. There was affection in it. Playfulness. A willingness to be a little silly in a room where people generally have other things on their minds. And James had something to give him, too. The photographs hold their back-and-forth. 06The warmth I remember. 07An ordinary errand. One of my favorite memories. Less than a week after this outing, James began having seizures. They are now under control with the care of the wonderful team at Mass General, and I am deeply grateful. That timing gives these photographs another layer of meaning for me. I come back to James’s part in all of this: his attention, his movement, the way he answered a gesture with one of his own. He and the guard made those 39 minutes together. I’m grateful I got to watch, and that these photographs let me revisit it. The people we meet are among the most profoundly AUsome parts of this life. Some stay. Some share a small stretch of it with us, and we carry that stretch for years.I hope this guard knows how much those minutes meant. I hope he knows that, somewhere, a mother still looks at these photographs and remembers how warmly he welcomed her son.There are so many things I want for James as he moves through the world. Friendship. Affection. The freedom to enjoy himself. People who notice what he is offering and respond.I got to watch that happen at the RMV.Thirty-nine minutes. Very few words. One of my favorite memories ever. The world isn’t always this AUsome. But when it is, it really is. With a parent guide to least restrictive environment.An AUsome Life · October 26, 2026 James at the beach. October 2026. Watching James at the beach yesterday, I wished Roseanne B. could see him. He was moving across the sand, safely, without an adult right at his side. I was there, watching—and feeling profoundly grateful to the special education director I once thought I was at war with. Roseanne had decades of experience. She would come to mean a great deal to me. But when I asked for James to have a one-on-one aide, we disagreed. I believed he needed someone specifically assigned to him. James has substantial support needs, and I wanted to be sure someone would notice when he needed help. Having an adult beside him seemed like the clearest way to make that happen. She declined. She explained her concern that, for James, the arrangement I was requesting could be more restrictive than he needed. At the time, that was hard to take in. I was asking for more help. How could that limit him? Many parents will recognize the feeling. You know school districts have finite resources, and you know your child's needs do not conveniently fit within them. It can be difficult to hear a refusal without feeling that you need to push harder. I was trying to protect my son. I still am. The principle behind our disagreement Roseanne was referring to least restrictive environment, or LRE, a requirement under the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA). In plain language, schools must educate children with disabilities alongside children without disabilities to the maximum extent appropriate. Before moving a child into a separate setting, the team must consider whether education in a general education classroom can work satisfactorily with supplementary aids and services.1 That support is part of the requirement. It can enable a child to participate in classrooms, extracurricular activities, and other parts of school life.2 A one-on-one aide is not automatically a more restrictive placement. For some children, an aide makes inclusion possible. Decisions about support must be grounded in the individual child's needs.13 What I appreciate now is the care that question deserved: how could James receive the help he needed while also having opportunities to initiate, make choices, and use his developing skills? I understand better why Roseanne wanted us to consider how the support would work in practice. Looking back, I am grateful for the experience she brought to that conversation. Watching him move across the sand brought that earlier conversation back to me. What stayed with me yesterday At the beach, I was thinking about James and the space around him. About being there, paying attention, while he moved without someone immediately beside him. School placement law does not tell a parent how far away to stand on a beach. But the question Roseanne helped me consider has stayed with me beyond school: where does James need our help, and where can we give him room? That answer changes with the situation. Yesterday, I could see what that room meant. I wanted him to have the support he needed. I wanted him to have this freedom, too. I thought of Roseanne, and of the whole village around James: the teachers, aides, therapists, and family members who have helped him learn and grow. So many people contribute to a child's life through patient, everyday care. And there was James, using his skills. Moving across the sand. Enjoying his day. I was proud of him, and grateful for the people who have supported him along the way. The people who help our children grow do not always get to see the moments their care has helped make possible. A school conversation can stay with a parent long after the meeting ends. Yesterday, on a beach, I felt a deeper appreciation for one of ours. It takes a village. Sometimes you feel the work of that village in a moment when your child has a little more room around him, and you can watch what he does with it. I once thought Roseanne and I were on opposite sides. Yesterday, I wished she could see James enjoying that space, and know how grateful I am for what she helped me understand. Roseanne, I thought of you yesterday. Thank you for being part of our village. Open the sections that are useful to you. What does the law protect—and why does it matter?IDEA gives eligible children a right to a free appropriate public education, commonly called FAPE. Its LRE provisions protect their opportunity to learn alongside peers without disabilities, with appropriate support, rather than being separated by default.14A child's placement must be based on their IEP and determined by a group that includes parents and people knowledgeable about the child, evaluation information, and placement options. The team must also consider possible harmful effects on the child or the quality of services.3The goal is an appropriate education with meaningful opportunities to participate. Being physically present in a classroom does not, by itself, explain whether a child's educational needs are being met. Does least restrictive mean fewer services?No. Supplementary aids and services are part of IDEA's approach to inclusion. They can support participation in regular classes and other school activities.2For some children, individual adult assistance helps them access instruction, communication, personal care, or activities. An aide is a support, not automatically a separate educational placement. The team needs to consider what the child requires and how the assistance will be provided.15A practical concern about excessive prompting or adult proximity should be examined in the child's actual circumstances. It is not a blanket reason to withhold needed help. Five questions for your next IEP meetingStart with the need. Which parts of the day are difficult? What observations or assessments show where support is required?Ask for specifics. If the team says an aide would be more restrictive, which opportunities might be limited, and what evidence supports that concern for your child?Examine the proposed alternative. Who will provide help, when will they be available, and what happens if they are absent?Include your child's communication. Consider preferences expressed through speech, AAC, gestures, expressions, and other communication.Plan how to review it. What information will show whether the arrangement is working? When will the team meet again?These are discussion prompts. The IEP itself must specify services and supports, anticipated frequency, location and duration, and how progress toward annual goals will be measured.5 What if the district says no—or cites limited resources?Ask for the educational reasons and the information behind the decision. Expertise matters, and parents deserve an explanation grounded in their child's needs.When a district refuses a requested change concerning identification, evaluation, placement, or provision of FAPE, IDEA requires prior written notice. It must explain the refusal, the assessments or records used, and the other options considered and rejected.6Staffing or resource shortages do not erase a district's obligation to provide FAPE in the least restrictive environment.7My gratitude in this story reflects our family's experience. Parents who disagree with a decision can seek information and support through their state's parent training center, an advocate, or a qualified special education attorney. Where can families find help?Across the United States: the Center for Parent Information and Resources directory helps families find Parent Training and Information Centers and Community Parent Resource Centers in their state or territory.9In Massachusetts: Massachusetts DESE's Families & Guardians page links to the state parent guide, procedural safeguards, information about selecting an advocate, and family organizations.The Federation for Children with Special Needs is another starting point for family information and support.8 A question to bring with you: “How will this plan meet my child's needs while supporting participation, choice, and opportunities to develop skills—and how will we know whether it is working?” Law and parent resources 34 CFR § 300.114 — Least restrictive environment requirements. 34 CFR § 300.42 — Supplementary aids and services. 34 CFR § 300.116 — Individualized placement decisions and parent involvement. summary: Our Wicked Tulips family photographs: spring color, a portrait and a practical note about enjoying a flower farm at your own pace.

title: Wicked Whoopies: a little stop with a very large whoopie pie.
summary: A family visit to Wicked Whoopies in Freeport, Maine: James, giant whoopie-pie displays, a colorful shop and useful sensory and access planning notes.
search: Freeport, Maine · From the family album Wicked Whoopies: a little stop with a very large whoopie pie. Orange walls, turquoise chairs, and a stack of whoopie pies taller than James. A Maine treat stop with a sense of humor. October 16, 2026 · A family visit The full-size James and the considerably oversized whoopie pies. From our family camera roll. A shop with a tower of whoopie pies has made its intentions quite clear. We are here for something sweet, and nobody is taking the décor too seriously. Our visit to Wicked Whoopies in Freeport, Maine, gave us exactly the sort of photographs I love keeping: James in his pink shirt, a wrapped treat in hand, standing beside a display that is delightfully out of proportion. The room is full of color. Orange walls, purple shelving, turquoise tables and chairs, blue flowers, and enormous red letters spelling “SMILE.” It is cheerful, a little theatrical, and thoroughly committed to its subject. A whoopie pie apparently deserves a pedestal. Several, in fact. James wore his hearing protection, as you can see in the photographs. That belongs in the family album just as much as the treat and the pink shirt. The pictures also give another family a useful preview of the bright interior before deciding whether it looks like their kind of stop. Plenty of color, right down to the shelving. This wider view is useful if you like to see a place before arriving. What makes this worth considering is its scale as an outing. You can build a small plan around a treat shop without needing a whole afternoon of activities. A browse, a choice, a photograph if everyone wants one, and then on with the day. My favorite detail is the contrast between the whoopie pie in James’s hand and the enormous versions behind him. One for the road; several that would require a moving van. Keep the plan small. Show the shop photographs beforehand if a preview helps. Bring the hearing protection or communication supports your family usually uses. If a particular flavor matters, call before making the trip: the shop’s selection can differ from the online store. There were tables and chairs in the shop when these photos were taken. You can ask about seating when you call, or plan to take your purchase with you. A short visit is a perfectly reasonable plan. A smaller stack, and another picture worth keeping. The useful details. Sound and light: Expect a visually busy setting: saturated colors, oversized displays and bright overhead lighting. The photographs cannot tell us how loud the shop will be during your visit. Ask the shop about quieter times if that would help. Mobility and facilities: Our photos show indoor seating and the shop floor, but do not establish step-free entry, doorway clearance, accessible parking or restroom facilities. Call the store about the specific route and facilities you need. Food: Wicked Whoopies’ current FAQ says it does not offer gluten-free or vegan whoopie pies. Check ingredients and any allergy or cross-contact questions directly before buying. Read the shop’s FAQ ↗ Put it in the address book. title: A camping swing, very much at home.
summary: Our portable Walmart swing, Yankee frugality, and autism-and-camping planning: familiar comforts, communication and room for a shorter trip. Original family photo.
search: Portable for camping · A little Yankee frugalityA camping swing, very much at home.Made for the campsite. Claimed by the stuffed animals. Our portable Walmart camping swing has earned its place at home, too—with a few thoughts on autism, camping, and bringing familiar comforts along.October 21, 2026 · From the family notebookOur Walmart camping swing, already full of stuffed animals, just after we moved in. Excuse the older photograph from just after we moved in, but this is one of those finds worth showing before the room is ready for its close-up. We love this swing. The stuffed animals seem fairly committed to it, too. It came from Walmart, and it was made for camping: an Ozark Trail hammock-style chair with its own folding frame. Not an elaborate installation. Not something that needed a dedicated room. Just a portable chair that turned out to be a very welcome part of our home. A little Yankee frugality. Yes, from Walmart.Our version of Yankee frugality is not about making life smaller. It is about getting good use out of what we bring into it. Does it work? Will we actually use it? Do we already own something that does the job?Something does not become less useful because it came from Walmart, or more useful because it came from a specialty catalog. A good find is a good find. We can appreciate a lovely old quilt and a practical camping chair in the same room. Neither needs to apologize for the other.Nor is thrift simply a contest to pay the least. The bargain that sits unused is not much of a bargain. A chair made for camping that also becomes a favorite at home has a rather better argument for its place.That is the appeal here: not buying a whole new room, not replacing something because it is no longer new, and not confusing an impressive label with a useful object. Just noticing what works for your family and continuing to enjoy it. The price tag is not the point. The life you get out of a thing is. Find it at Walmart.Check the blue Ozark Trail hammock-chair listing ↗Availability note, October 21, 2026: The blue listing showed shipping, pickup and delivery unavailable when checked. It remains useful for identifying the chair and reading reviews, but it is not a promise that you can order it today.Browse Walmart’s current hammock-chair listings ↗. Our photograph shows an earlier purchase, not a guarantee of an identical production version. Compare the exact model, seller, instructions, price and availability before ordering. The portable part is the point.This is camping furniture, and that is part of its appeal. Walmart’s description for this model lists a folding frame and an included carry bag for transport and storage. The chair can come along with the camping gear instead of being a permanent fixture.That is worth knowing whether your interest is campsite seating or a chair you can put away when you need the space. Our own photograph and firsthand story are from home; this is not a campsite field test.Other owners have plenty to say, too. On October 21, 2026, Walmart’s listing showed 4.3 out of 5 stars from 466 ratings. Positive reviews describe easy setup and comfort; not every owner agrees about the fit. Read the critical reviews as well as the enthusiastic ones. That is the retailer’s listing score, not our own testing score, and it can change. A favorite does not need a specialty label.At our house, the cozy, swing-style seat found a place among James’s favorite stuffed animals. We pay attention to what he actually enjoys, not only what a product label says it is supposed to do.Sometimes the useful things are specialized. Sometimes they are in the camping aisle. We are glad we found this one. A seat full of stuffed animals is not a showroom photograph, but it is a fairly good picture of something having found its place. Autism and camping: bring a little familiar with you. A change of scenery does not have to mean changing every familiar thing. That is the camping connection this chair makes us think about: a comfortable place someone already enjoys might be something to bring along, when it suits both the person and the setting. Start with the autistic person, not an “autism-friendly” shopping list. A child, teenager or adult might enjoy a moving seat, prefer a firm, still chair, or choose something else entirely. Their preferences come first. Our chair is a home favorite; the suggestions here are for planning, not an account of taking it camping. Try the smaller version. Explore the equipment at home, or consider a short outdoor visit before committing to an overnight. Sitting outside together can be the whole plan. Nobody has to graduate to a tent. Preview the everyday details. Look at campsite photographs and maps together. Ask about bathrooms, paths, lighting, neighboring sites and noise. Plan around the person’s actual access and sensory needs, rather than assuming outdoors always means quiet. Bring what already works. Familiar food, bedding or a preferred comfort item may be worth the packing space. Keep the person’s usual communication available, including AAC—augmentative and alternative communication—where used. Plan charging, weather protection and a familiar backup; a “screen-free” trip must not mean losing a way to communicate. Keep choices real. Leave time for pauses and a quieter place to go. Respect “no,” “break” and “all done,” however they are communicated. A shorter visit or going home is an option, not a failed outing. For a person who needs substantial support, include personal care, overnight support and an individual safety plan in the arrangements. Plan for water, roads, fire, weather and emergencies; do not assume mobile service will be available. A familiar chair cannot replace those supports. And there is our Yankee-frugality point again: begin with the person’s familiar things, not a new cartful of “sensory camping essentials.” Planning references, checked October 21, 2026: National Autistic Society: holiday planning for autistic people and families, and National Park Service: before a camping trip. These are general planning resources, not endorsements of this chair. For something you can adapt to your own day, try our visual visit planner or AAC-friendly outing note. A few details before you settle in.Check the instructions, assembly, weight limit and intended movement for the exact chair you buy. Use a level, clear space and keep loose cords away from the frame and entry path; our moving-in photograph is a family snapshot, not a recommended setup. A camping chair is not automatically a therapeutic swing or suitable for every person. title: A Love Letter to Buying Nothing
summary: A framed Boston alphabet from a local Buy Nothing group, Yankee thrift, and the art of neighborly generosity. Plus a searchable New England sharing and swap shed directory.
search: A family note · October 2026A Love Letter to Buying NothingOn Yankee thrift, the kindness of neighbors, and the beautiful things we pass along.An AUsome Life · New EnglandA framed print, a local Buy Nothing group, and a very good reminder that free need not mean ordinary.Our Boston alphabet print, shared by a neighbor through a local Buy Nothing group. Family photograph; the artwork bears a Mr. Boddington credit. The latest addition to our home came already framed: a Boston alphabet, from Frog Pond to the Zakim Bridge, surrounded by a generous green mat and a white frame that has plainly seen some life. Which, really, is part of the point.We found it through our local Buy Nothing group. Someone had something worth enjoying and offered it to a neighbor. We happened to be the neighbors who brought it home.It's not just the sort of thing I would happily admire in a shop. It's the sort of thing that makes a room feel like the people who live there actually live there. A little Boston, letter by letter.There is a joke tucked into nearly every square. A is for Arabesque on Frog Pond—which sent us straight back to our own Boston Common Frog Pond guide. F is for Fall at Faneuil Hall. There is the Green Monster, Make Way for the Ducklings, and the Red Line. Newbury Street gets the caption “Not Cheap,” which is a good joke for a picture that came home free.That this print came to us through a neighbor makes us treasure it all the more.To me, that's good Yankee frugality. Not refusing to enjoy beautiful things. Not turning household life into a competition to spend the least. It's appreciating what's already here, knowing the difference between price and value, and being delighted when a useful or lovely thing finds the right person. The best things in a home are not always the things we went shopping for. The joy of receiving matters, too.We talk about the pleasure of giving, and rightly so. But Buy Nothing communities ask us to be comfortable on both sides of the exchange.One week, perhaps you are the person with a lamp to spare. Another week, you are the person who could really use one. A borrowed folding table, a box of books, an extra frame, a garden tool you only need twice: these things don't have to sit in a cupboard waiting to be useful someday.And neither does kindness have to be a grand gesture. It can be a simple message, a good photograph of the item, a cheerful pickup, and an uncomplicated thank-you.There's dignity in being able to ask. And there's something heartening about a community where a person who receives today is never expected to justify their need or become a charity project. Because ordinary life has an extraordinary bill.Most families know the arithmetic of daily life: groceries, housing, school supplies, the car, the utility bill that arrived at an especially inconvenient moment. For many disabled people and families caring for disabled relatives, there can be another layer—medical bills, therapy, adaptive equipment, transportation, appointments, and the work hours that become difficult to keep.A free household item will not fix those larger pressures. Nor should neighborly generosity be used as an excuse for systems that fail to provide people with what they need. But it can ease one small expense, save one trip, or simply make an ordinary Tuesday a little nicer.And everyone belongs in these groups—not only people who are struggling financially. When households with different resources all give and receive freely, the exchange becomes a way of living together rather than a label about who needs help.It can mean choosing a beautiful framed print while keeping money for a medical bill, a family outing, the occasional good meal, or whatever makes a particular household's life work. No one should have to choose between necessity and every bit of everyday pleasure. A rather good version of the American life.We often talk about the good American life as something we acquire: the right house, the right furnishings, the right things inside it. I think there's another version worth holding on to. It's a home that feels welcoming, enough time with the people you love, a little freedom from waste and worry, and neighbors who remember that we need one another.It feels very New England to me, with the practical affection for old things, shared tools, and a sturdy frame. But the idea belongs everywhere. Every town could use a few more people willing to pass something along.There is a conservation story here, too. Reuse is not quite the same as recycling: it means keeping a perfectly serviceable thing in use rather than processing its materials. Connecticut’s Department of Energy and Environmental Protection explains the distinction. One picture changing walls will not save the planet, but it belongs to a habit that keeps good things in circulation.So here is to the generous neighbor, the well-used swap shed, the free book left for the next reader, and the perfectly good thing that doesn't need another trip to the store.And here's to our Boston alphabet, a lovely little reminder that value and price were never synonyms in the first place.The letter is personal; the guide below is practical. You'll find verified links to free-sharing groups and town reuse programs throughout New England. Worth saving · worth sharingYour Guide to Yankee FrugalityNot a prescription to do without. A handful of generous, useful habits for enjoying what we already have—and leaving a little more room for what matters. 01Ask your neighbors first.Before buying the extra tray, picture frame, bookshelf or garden tool, see whether someone nearby has one they're happy to give. A polite ask can save money and start a conversation.02Offer it while it is still good.A clean, complete, working item is a gift. Mention its condition honestly, including any flaws. Nobody needs a mystery repair project unless they want one.03Find the town swap shed.Many New England towns have reuse sheds or swap shops at recycling centers. Some are volunteer-run or seasonal, and many require a resident sticker. Always check first.04Borrow the once-a-year thing.Ask your library about a Library of Things; try borrowing the telescope, sewing machine, power tool, or board game before buying one to store for years.05Make pickup easy for real people.Give clear directions, communicate about timing, and consider transportation and accessibility needs. A free item loses its charm if collecting it becomes an obstacle course.06Receive without apology.People share because they want the item used. You don't have to explain your finances. The details that make an outing possible “Accessible” can mean almost nothing until somebody tells you about the hill, the gravel, the elevator, the lighting, the quiet corner, the restroom and the walk from the car. This is the standard we use when researching calendar events, Favorite Places and practical guides. We look for current official information first, then use public visitor reports as a secondary reality check when they add useful lived detail. We label uncertainty instead of turning it into a promise. What we checkEight questions before “accessible.”Not every venue publishes every answer. An honest “not confirmed” is more useful than a confident guess. Wheelchair + adaptive strollerStep-free entrances, ramps, elevators, doorway routes, seating, transfer points, wheelchair or mobility-device rentals and whether the route actually works beyond the lobby. Terrain + distancePavement, packed gravel, loose gravel, grass, roots, slopes, long walks, mud, snow and places where a wheeled mobility device may need more help than a general accessibility label suggests. Sensory + communicationNoise, lighting, crowd density, smells, startling effects, quiet spaces, sensory kits, visual supports, AAC-friendly participation, flexible movement, re-entry and whether “sensory-friendly” changes the environment or only the schedule. Blind + low-vision accessBraille, large print, tactile or verbal description, audio description, contrast, wayfinding and lighting changes. We avoid assuming that a wheelchair-accessible route is also an accessible visual experience. Deaf + hard-of-hearing accessCaptions, ASL interpretation, assistive-listening systems, visual announcements, hearing loops/headsets and how far in advance an accommodation must be requested. Restrooms + practical careAccessible and family restrooms, changing tables, and an adult-size or height-adjustable changing table only when a venue specifically publishes that information. We never imply that a particular family uses a facility simply because we report that it exists. Parking + arrivalAccessible spaces, drop-off, distance to the entrance, the best door to use, city parking realities, whether a shuttle runs and what happens after dark. Weather + escape planOutdoor exposure, snow, ice, rain, heat, muddy paths, low light, indoor backup options, break spaces and how easy it is to shorten the visit or leave. Evidence labels How strong is the information? Organizer-confirmedA current event page, ticket page, venue policy or direct accessibility statement. This is our starting point. Venue access guideA current accessibility, visitor, trail, seating or building guide that adds detail beyond the event listing. Public visitor reportA review or public Q&A can reveal practical realities—steepness, crowd bottlenecks, muddy ground, stroller frustration—but it is anecdotal and dated. We label it as such and do not let it override newer official information. Not confirmedWe looked and did not find a reliable current answer. That is a prompt to contact the venue, not permission to guess. See the method in useThe calendar now carries the field notes.Each dated listing can include mobility, terrain, sensory conditions, vision/hearing supports, restrooms, changing-equipment status, parking, weather, a map and a five-step visual visit card.Open the accessible New England calendar ↗ Editorial rules What we will not do. We do not convert “ADA accessible” into a blanket promise about the whole experience. We do not assume a venue has an adult-size changing table, sensory room, ASL interpreter, elevator or smooth terrain unless we can confirm it. We do not present a visitor review as a verified current venue policy. We date access research because buildings, programs, construction, staffing and weather conditions change. We do not diagnose what a person “should” need. The information is there so each reader can decide what matters for their own visit. The website itself Access should apply here, too. We aim for readable type, strong contrast, keyboard-accessible navigation, useful headings, meaningful link text, alt text for informative images, layouts that work on smaller screens, and controls that do not rely on color alone. Visual planners are editable because one person’s helpful wording or picture can be another person’s clutter. Our tools use visible words alongside icons, large controls, familiar examples, keyboard access and clear optional sections. Preselected settings make it possible to finish without adjusting every detail. Color choices always have written names; color alone does not carry an instruction. Our creative standardBeautiful, useful, respectful.Our default look is preppy New England: Nantucket light, Vermont warmth, recognizable objects and natural materials. Communication pictures keep a clear subject and a familiar word. Decoration belongs around the task, where it can add pleasure without obscuring meaning.We create and publish lawful, family-friendly content. Sexual content, graphic violence, hate imagery, exploitation, harassment and deceptive images of real people have no place here. We respect privacy, consent, intellectual property and the dignity of the people we portray. AI-created illustrations are identified as such and are never presented as family photographs or evidence about a real venue.The picture-card studio currently offers a reviewed starter collection and private, in-tab photo selection. It has no public upload gallery and does not generate new images live. Personal photos are not sent to us or automatically inspected. Use only appropriate pictures you are permitted to use. Any future live image-generation service must include input and output moderation before it is made available. title: Tourists in Our Own Backyard
summary: A writer, a professor, and an overdue mid-fall date at Authors’ Ridge in Concord. Our photographs and watercolors, local history, a map, and practical access notes.
search: Concord, Massachusetts · Time for two Tourists in Our Own Backyard A mid-fall date at Authors’ Ridge. A writer, a professor, three years living nearby—and a little literary pilgrimage we somehow hadn’t made. Our photographs, watercolors, local history, and the practical details for a visit of your own. October 21, 2026 · An AUsome Life Louisa May Alcott’s resting place, from our own visit to Authors’ Ridge. I’m a writer. Dad is a professor. We’d lived here for three years.And somehow, we had never made the trek to Authors’ Ridge. On paper, we were very well qualified to have done this already. But a funny thing happens when you live near somewhere people travel to see: it becomes the place you can visit any time. And “any time” has a way of slipping behind everything that actually has a date on the calendar. So, for a little while this fall, we became tourists in our own backyard. Our date took us to Authors’ Ridge in Concord’s Sleepy Hollow Cemetery, where Louisa May Alcott, Henry David Thoreau, Nathaniel Hawthorne and Ralph Waldo Emerson are buried. Familiar names, suddenly attached to very small, very human places. About the writers and the cemetery. The things people leave behind Look closely at the photographs. Around Louisa May Alcott’s marker are pencils, pinecones, stones and a pink rose. At Thoreau’s, more pencils lie among the roots and needles, beneath a little stone that simply says Henry. I find the pencils especially moving. Such ordinary things, brought to the graves of people whose words have lasted so long. To me, they look like small thank-yous: your work reached someone. Someone is still reading. Hawthorne’s marker has its own quiet simplicity. A rounded stone, a surname, sunlight and shadow. You can know a name for years and still feel differently about it when you stand in front of it, outdoors, at the scale of a person. Henry: a small marker, tree roots, and the things visitors have left. Hawthorne, in patches of sun and shade. In our photographs, the trees still hold plenty of green. A little gold is beginning to show. The ground has its own autumn palette: brown needles, gray stone, moss, a bright flower. There is enough to look at before you read a single name. Before the graves, there were evening walks One of my favorite pieces of this place’s history is that the writers knew it as a place to walk. The National Park Service records that Emerson, Thoreau, and Nathaniel and Sophia Hawthorne enjoyed evening walks in Sleepy Hollow before it became a cemetery. Before these woods held their graves, they held their evening walks. That makes a date here feel part of a much older habit: going outside together, looking around, letting a familiar landscape give you something to think about. Sleepy Hollow was dedicated on September 29, 1855, with an address by Emerson. Landscape architects Horace William Shaler Cleveland and Robert Morris Copeland planned paths and drives around the natural shape of the land, respecting its trees and plants. The Concord Free Public Library’s dedication exhibit describes that approach—and notes that the place already carried the name Sleepy Hollow before it was a burial ground. It belongs to the nineteenth-century tradition of rural or garden cemeteries, where landscape and remembrance meet. The winding roads and wooded setting are part of the history you have come to see. Read about the landscape. A little more of the neighborhood Concord’s history reaches much further back than the writers. The Concord Museum identifies the area as the original homelands of the Nipmuc, Massachusett and Pawtucket tribal nations, and recognizes Indigenous people’s continuing connection to this land. Nearby, the North Bridge holds another chapter: the battle of April 19, 1775. A visit to Concord can open onto many histories. Authors’ Ridge gave us plenty to notice on its own. Something lovely, close to home A date like this makes room for the people we are as well as the people we look after. I’m still a writer. Dad is still someone who loves ideas. And we are still two people who can go somewhere together and find things worth noticing. I like that the visit didn’t need to be elaborate to be worth remembering. A nearby place, a little curiosity, a few photographs. There is a particular pleasure in finally doing the thing that has been waiting so close to home. Three years was a long time to get around to it. I’m glad we finally went. From the photographsA little autumn sketchbook Three watercolor interpretations of our visit. The photographs above show the actual places; these companion illustrations hold their color and feeling. About our editorial artwork. Louisa May Alcott · Original editorial illustration Henry David Thoreau · Original editorial illustration Nathaniel Hawthorne · Original editorial illustration For a visit of your ownFind the hillside—and your way around Open location map ↗Get directions ↗ This map locates the destination. It does not verify a step-free route, a usable parking space, or the condition of a cemetery path. Inside Sleepy Hollow Authors’ Ridge, Sleepy Hollow Cemetery Bedford Street, Concord, Massachusetts. The town’s detailed map labels the gates, internal roads, paths and graves of interest. Open it before you arrive, and use current signs on the grounds. Open the official cemetery map (PDF) ↗ Arriving by car: the town’s visitor brochure directs drivers approaching from the center toward the second Bedford Street gate and notes parking near Authors’ Ridge. That brochure is older; follow current gate and parking signs and keep the roads clear. Town visitor guide. For current gate, parking or route questions, call the Cemetery Office: 978-318-3233. The practical details left inPlan a visit that works for you Cost: free to visit, according to Visit Concord.Hours: town rules list daily opening at 7 a.m. and closing at dusk or 8 p.m., whichever comes first, weather permitting. In mid-fall, plan around the earlier dusk. Check current town rules and posted gate signs. Mobility, ground surfaces & the approach Authors’ Ridge is a hillside visit. The official tourism listing says the approach includes an incline. Our photographs show exposed roots, bare earth and pine needles around some markers. The town’s cemetery master plan acknowledges accessibility challenges from the hills and limited parking. Parking nearer the ridge may shorten the approach; it does not establish a level or step-free route to every grave. If you use a wheelchair, walker or stroller, or need to limit walking, ask the Cemetery Office about your specific route and parking needs before going: 978-318-3233. After rain, take extra care around wet leaves and roots. Restrooms & a place to regroup Plan a restroom stop in Concord Center. The Concord Visitor Center at 58 Main Street lists public bathrooms, and its access guide identifies accessible restrooms inside. Those two pages currently give different opening hours for the facilities. If access to a particular restroom matters to your visit, call 978-318-3061 to confirm availability. Sensory needs, pacing & family planning The photos here are from our date. They do not establish how this outing would work for another person or at another time. Outdoor space can still include other visitors, vehicles and maintenance sounds. title: Old friends, an autumn wedding & a weekend away.
summary: An autumn wedding in New Haven, old college friends from Bristol and Rome, a little time away, and the grandparents who made it possible.
search: From the autumn camera roll · New Haven, Connecticut Old friends, an autumn wedding & a weekend away. College friends from Bristol and Rome, a wonderful wedding, a downtown hotel, and a little time to ourselves. A November 2018 memory · Shared October 22, 2026 All dressed up for a lovely autumn weekend. I've been loving all the old autumn photos that keep resurfacing on my phone lately. Every few days, another little memory pops up — a place we visited, people we love, or a wonderful weekend I'd nearly forgotten about. And these photographs from November 2018 took me right back to New Haven, Connecticut. We were there to celebrate the wedding of our dear friends Deb and Artur, and it was such a lovely excuse to reconnect with college friends from my years in Bristol, Rhode Island, and Rome, Italy. ❤️ There are some friendships that will always remind you of a particular time in your life — the places you went, the adventures you had, and the person you were back then. Seeing everyone again was such a treat. A sweet New England wedding detail, right down to the date on the maple-leaf bottle. A weekend away takes a village. Of course, leaving James for a weekend is never particularly easy for me. As many parents and caregivers know, even the loveliest getaway comes with a fair amount of planning (and perhaps a little worrying!). Thankfully, James was in wonderful hands with Mom-Mom and Grandpa Steve, who love him beyond measure and have always been such an important part of our village. Knowing he was with people who know and adore him made it easier to enjoy a little grown-up time. ❤️ We stayed at the beautiful Omni New Haven Hotel at Yale, right downtown. It was such a treat to enjoy a lovely hotel, explore New Haven in autumn, catch up with old friends, and have a little time away from our everyday routines. And the New Haven pizza? Oh, my goodness. 🍕 That's a whole 'nother delicious story, and one that absolutely deserves its own post! Old friends, dressed for the occasion. A heartfelt family remembrance among the wedding details. Dessert, with a side of disco lighting. There may have been some spectacular fashion choices. And yes, the novelty hats came out. 😂 The people are the best part. Deb and Artur's wedding was beautiful, with heartfelt family tributes, wonderful food, lots of laughter, and some truly spectacular fashion choices once the novelty hats and oversized sunglasses made their appearance. But I think what I loved most was simply being together again. There is something so special about friendships that stretch across years, countries, and completely different chapters of life. The people who knew you when you were young and figuring everything out, and who still feel like old friends no matter how much time has passed. And as much as I love sharing adventures with James, these occasional grown-up getaways are part of our story, too. Being a caregiver is a huge part of my life, but so are the friendships, places, memories, and experiences that have helped make me who I am. One more thing worth rememberingGood people make room for good weekends. This getaway was possible because Mom-Mom and Grandpa Steve could be there for James. That kind of trusted family support matters, and I never take it for granted. Not every family has it; it's one reason I believe time for caregivers, and real support to make it possible, is so important. I'm so glad these photos found their way back onto my phone this autumn. A lovely reminder of a beautiful weekend, two wonderful people, and friendships I'm very grateful to have made along the way. ❤️ Here's to Deb and Artur, old friends, and all the stories that follow us home. 🍁 Explore related topics Places & outings Travel & stays

title: A little Bristol blue.
summary: A family photograph from Bristol, Rhode Island, a short waterfront guide, and our experience practicing staying together safely.
search: The journalBristol, Rhode IslandFrom the family archives · October 19, 2026 An afternoon by the harborA little Bristol blue.Sailboats, stripes, and a much smaller James. A photograph from the family album, with a short guide for an afternoon on the waterfront.Looking through old photos and found this one. Apparently, we all got the memo about wearing blue.The three of us by the water. From an earlier family visit. Glad we took this one.Bristol, Rhode Island: sailboats, sparkling water, and a family afternoon by the harbor. There is James in front, with the boats behind us and the sun on the water.There is a practical detail in the photograph, too. James and I were each holding a voluntary walking handle as we practiced staying together safely. Nothing was attached to him; there was no tether or restraint, and he could let go at any time.For our family, it was one way to practice while getting out and enjoying the community. Every child and family has different needs, and what worked for us may not feel right or be appropriate for someone else. It was one small part of our experience, alongside close supervision.Mostly, I am glad we have this picture. An afternoon by the water with my two favorite people. Original editorial illustration, inspired by Bristol. An imagined harbor scene, separate from our family photograph. A small plan for a day outAlong the waterfront.These are researched ideas for a visit today, rather than a list of places we visited on the afternoon in our photograph.Start at Independence Park.At 419–459 Thames Street, this four-acre park overlooks Bristol Harbor and marks the southern end of the East Bay Bike Path. The state tourism listing includes walkways and public restrooms; check restroom availability for your visit. A good starting point for watching the boats without committing to a long walk.Independence Park visitor informationTake a waterfront wander.The town points visitors to the boardwalk behind Stone Harbour condominiums, leading toward Rockwell Park and the Maritime Center. Choose a short stretch, stop for the view, and turn back whenever you like.Bristol’s official places guideTry a little of the bike path.The East Bay Bike Path runs 13.8 miles between Providence and Bristol. You do not have to tackle the whole thing: a short out-and-back from Independence Park can be enough. Cyclists share the path, so plan the support and space your family needs.East Bay Bike Path detailsMake Audubon a separate stop.The Audubon Nature Center and Aquarium at 1401 Hope Street has exhibits, walking trails and a boardwalk toward Narragansett Bay. Audubon describes its facility and trails as accessible. Check opening hours, admission and closure announcements before heading over.Audubon visitor informationBefore you go: check parking signs, restroom access and waterfront conditions. Bristol announced funding for seawall work at Independence Park and the Maritime Center in October 2026; the notice does not establish a closure schedule, so check local updates before visiting. Waterfront routes can include open edges, docks and boat activity.Official visitor sources checked October 19, 2026. This is a family recollection with a researched guide, not a current accessibility audit. Town seawall project notice. About the walking handle & practicing staying together safelyWe each held part of the handle, with James choosing to hold his. It gave us a way to practice walking together. Unexpected separation can become dangerous quickly, even with attentive caregivers.A similar style is called Hold-On Handles. This link shows the type of product, not a confirmed match for ours; current stock and suitability need checking.In a 2012 parent survey involving 1,218 autistic children, 49% were reported to have attempted elopement at least once after age four. That describes the surveyed group, not any individual child’s future. Read the original study in Pediatrics.The practical, hopeful part is making room for learning and finding supports that fit. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends teaching safety skills alongside consistent adult supervision and an individual safety plan. Read the AAP’s guidance for families.A voluntarily held handle can be released at any moment. It cannot prevent unexpected separation or replace close supervision, particularly near water or traffic. We are sharing our experience, not general advice or a recommendation for restraint. Neither source establishes that a walking handle reduces elopement.Different people need different supports. title: A little 1954 magic in Buenos Aires.
summary: Photos of Don Julio in Palermo, Buenos Aires, and the sweet 1954 tradition Mom-Mom and Grandpa Steve share before their Viking cruise.
search: Buenos Aires, Argentina · From the family camera rollA little 1954 magic in Buenos Aires.Mom-Mom and Grandpa Steve, a famous restaurant, and a very special number.A family travel note · October 2026One happy stop in Buenos Aires before the next adventure at sea. Mom-Mom and Grandpa Steve are off on another adventure! Before boarding their Viking cruise, they made a stop at Don Julio in Buenos Aires — a restaurant recommended by my colleagues in Argentina.And what a gorgeous place for a photograph. Green-and-white striped awnings, a beautiful old building, and pumpkins everywhere. They look almost like New England in October, even though it's spring in Buenos Aires.But one of my favorite pictures from this stop isn't of the restaurant at all. Another 1954 for their collection.Their little travel tradition1954.Mom-Mom and Steve were both born in 1954. Wherever they travel, if they spot that number on a building, sign, or street address, they take a photograph.A small souvenir from every place they find it. I love that they have this tradition — a little reminder of the year they both came into the world.Of all the things you can collect while traveling, I think this might be one of the sweetest. ❤️ A little adventure of their own.These two give so much love and time to James and their other grandchildren. They're part of the family village that makes so many of our days possible, particularly when life involves the extra planning and support James needs.They also love to travel. And I love seeing them out exploring together, doing something for themselves, collecting stories (and 1954s) along the way.Oh, and don't worry: Ruby was in very good hands while they were away. 🐾 The Don Julio storefront on a beautiful sunny day.Pumpkins in springtime, Buenos Aires style. A little connection back homeA taste of Argentina, by way of Maine.Speaking of Buenos Aires: if you'd like a taste of Argentina a little closer to home, Rococo Ice Cream in Kennebunk, Maine, has its own Argentine connection. Its founder spent time in Argentina, where the city's ice-cream culture helped inspire what became one of our family's favorite New England stops.Read our family's Rococo story, A scoop with a view → We have lots more to share from Mom-Mom and Steve's South American travels. For now, here's to a beautiful stop at Don Julio, a recommendation from colleagues halfway around the world, and another little piece of 1954 to add to the collection.May they find a thousand more. ❤️❤️ The 1954 photo tradition Have you ever found your year? title: Burlington, at our pace.
summary: Our Burlington, Vermont trip in family photographs: Oakledge’s accessible treehouse, pool time at The Essex, Al’s French Frys, and a little holiday sparkle.
search: Burlington & Essex, Vermont · From the family album Burlington, at our pace. A treehouse, a swim, a stop at Al’s, and a little holiday sparkle. The small pieces of a Vermont trip worth keeping. Published October 16, 2026 · Photographs from an earlier family trip Pool time at The Essex. One of the good parts of getting away. Looking back through our Burlington photographs, I keep coming back to the smaller scenes: James in his Vermont shirt, the red booths at Al’s, a tree growing straight through a treehouse, and the two of them together in the pool. There is a very good Vermont trip in those pictures. A little time outside. Something familiar to eat. Water to get into. A Christmas tree dressed in black-and-white checks, because apparently even the decorations had packed appropriately. For our family, those ordinary pieces deserve room in the story. James loves the water, and the swimming photographs belong right alongside the sightseeing ones. The pool is part of the trip. A swim at The Essex The indoor pool at The Essex Resort & Spa has a lovely setting: wood walls, white beams, large windows, and blue-green water. In our photographs, James is wearing his life jacket with his dad beside him. In another, the two of them are wrapped up in a poolside hug. The photograph I would keep even without a travel story attached.White robes, white columns, and a little Vermont sunshine. The covered walkway is another detail I like in the album: two white robes, a long row of columns, and stripes of sunlight across the path. It is a useful reminder to ask about the journey between a room and a pool. The Essex’s spa is in a separate building; the practical notes below include the resort’s current access information. A treehouse you can actually get into At Oakledge Park in Burlington, the treehouse is built around the tree itself. Thick branches frame the view; the floorboards and rustic railings make a little room in the woods. James’s orange jacket stands out against all that weathered wood. Inside Oakledge’s treehouse, with the tree very much part of the room.A place to stop and look out. The access is part of what makes this place worth knowing about. Its builders describe it as a universally accessible community treehouse, created with the City of Burlington. That matters: the experience of being up among the branches should have room for more people. Our photographs capture the inside, rather than the full approach. For a future visit, I would check the route and current conditions with the park, especially after wet or icy weather. A lovely wooden walkway still has to contend with Vermont. Red booths and a Vermont shirt Our stop at Al’s French Frys in South Burlington looks exactly like the sort of place you hope to find on a New England trip: red booths, little pendant lights, and a black-and-white tiled floor. James is standing by the table in his Vermont shirt, with his device close by. A Vermont shirt for a Vermont stop. Al’s French Frys, South Burlington. That is a useful little travel detail in its own right. A communication device belongs at the table, within reach. New surroundings need not mean leaving familiar supports behind. Al’s current menu lists its namesake fries alongside burgers, sandwiches, and ice cream. The photo is our souvenir of the stop; for a particular food preference or allergy, check the current menu and preparation details directly. A little holiday sparkle A grin, red ornaments, and rather good checked ribbon. And then there is this picture. James, smiling beside the Christmas tree, blue Crocs and all. The ribbon is coordinated. The family travel wardrobe is taking a more independent approach. Looking through this trip again, what stands out is the variety without the need for a grand production: the treehouse, the pool, the diner, the decorations. There is plenty here for a family album, and plenty to build a manageable Burlington visit around. Take the useful details with youPlanning your own version These are memories from an earlier trip. The venue details below were checked on October 16, 2026; they describe what the venues currently publish, rather than facilities we personally tested. The Essex Resort & Spa · 70 Essex Way, EssexThe resort lists a year-round indoor pool. Its accessibility page says the spa and fitness center are in a separate building with paved wheelchair access, and that the pools and whirlpool have lifts. Ask about the exact route from your room, lift availability, changing arrangements, and current family swimming hours. We did not test the lifts or accessible rooms. Oakledge Park · Flynn Avenue, BurlingtonThe treehouse is documented as a universally accessible community treehouse. Burlington’s parks guidance says it is first come, first served and must remain open to the public. Burlington Wildways lists parking and accessible spaces near the Greenway. Check current parking charges, restroom availability, and the condition of the treehouse approach before you go. Al’s French Frys · 1251 Williston Road, South BurlingtonOur photo shows indoor booth seating. It does not establish wheelchair clearance, restroom access, or typical sound levels. Call 802-862-9203 for the seating or access details your family needs, and check the current menu and hours. A simple plan Choose one main outing, leave room for swimming, and keep a food stop flexible. These places are in Burlington, South Burlington, and Essex, so allow for driving between them. The photographs are a collection of trip moments, not a timed itinerary. For us, a useful planning question is: what does everyone need in order to enjoy the part we came for? A place to change, a device within reach, time to linger, and permission to finish while the day is still going well. Our hotel and pool checklist can help with the calls before booking. For a shorter outing, start with the shorter-visit plan.
