title: Almost home.
summary: A decade in Burlington, a return from Massachusetts with James, and South Burlington’s whale tails: memories, parking, walking access and nearby I-89.
search: South Burlington, Vermont · From the family album Almost home.Burlington’s whale tails, then and now. A decade of lake days, friendship and belonging—and a return from Massachusetts with James. With parking, walking access and nearby-highway planning notes. An AUsome Life · Published October 22, 2026 · A memory from an earlier family visit James at the whale tails. An old sign of home, and a new family memory. For years, two whale tails sticking out of a Vermont field meant I was almost home. I lived in Burlington for a decade, and Lake Champlain was my everything. Being near the water brought me peace and helped ease my anxiety. I could look out over the lake and feel a little more room inside myself. That kind of comfort stays with you. My friends were just as much a part of what made it home. When I think about Burlington, the people and the place come together: the friendships, the lake, the feeling of belonging to a community. It is a community like no other I’ve known, surrounded by a beauty I still miss. That is what the whale tails were welcoming me back to. There they were beside I-89, familiar and wonderfully improbable. I couldn’t tell you how many times I passed them over those years. I can tell you what seeing them meant: nearly there. Back to the lake, my friends, my life. They are technically in South Burlington, but to me they belong to that feeling of arriving in Burlington. Two enormous whale tails in the grass. In Vermont. Of course. They are so perfectly Burlington: art out in the open, a little oddness, a love of the natural world, and something worth looking at on an otherwise ordinary drive. I love that they manage to be both a surprise and an old friend. Now home is in Massachusetts. Getting back to Vermont takes a little more doing, and being able to make that trek with James means a great deal to me. There is something wonderful about bringing your child to a place that already holds years of your life. You arrive with all those memories, and then you get to add him. That is what I see in this photograph. James on the green path, smiling, with tall grasses on either side and the whale tails up behind him. All that blue sky. A place I have carried around in my mind, with my son right there in the middle of it. For so long, the tails were something I passed on my way home. Getting out and walking toward them with James made them a destination in their own right. I love having a photograph of that. When I think of the whale tails now, I get to think of this day, too. The sculpture has a proper name: Reverence. Jim Sardonis created it in 1989, carving the tails from African black granite. They spent their first ten years in Randolph before moving to South Burlington in 1999. At roughly 12 to 13 feet high, they have a presence that a passing glimpse from the highway doesn’t quite convey.1, 2 And there really is a whale story beneath the Vermont landscape. The Champlain Valley was once occupied by the Champlain Sea. In 1849, railroad workers in nearby Charlotte uncovered the bones of a beluga whale. The University of Vermont tells the story of that discovery and the ancient sea that explains it.3 Whales in a Vermont field turn out to be a little less improbable than they first appear. I appreciate that history. I appreciate the sculpture. But my attachment to those tails is also very simple: I saw them over the years, and they came to mean home. Massachusetts is home now, too. Coming back with James lets those two parts of my life meet. I get to bring him into a place that gave me so much: friendship, beauty, and somewhere to find a little peace. I can be a visitor here and still feel the old recognition. There they are. I know this place. And now I have this picture of James to add to all the years before it. The practical detailsVisiting the whale tails Our photograph records an earlier visit. These planning notes were checked on October 22, 2026, using the artist’s directions, Technology Park and Trail Finder. Conditions and parking arrangements can change. Where to go & parkReverence is at Technology Park in South Burlington. Approach via Community Drive off Kimball Avenue; Trail Finder places the trailhead on the right as the road curves. Use designated trail parking and follow posted signs. Reach the walking route through Technology Park. Cost & walking distanceTrail Finder lists no fee and a 1.7-mile loop. That is the full listed loop, not a measured parking-to-sculpture distance. A Vermont Moms account describes a shorter walk directly to the tails. Follow the current marked route and turn back when it suits your family. Ground & mobility accessThe listed surfaces are grass/meadow and packed earth/dirt. Our photo shows the uphill grassy approach. Trail Finder rates the route “easy,” but wheelchair and stroller suitability depends on the device, slope and ground conditions. A paved accessible route, accessible parking bays and visitor toilets were not confirmed in the sources checked. Comfort & planningOur photo shows an exposed stretch with little shade. Bring water and weather protection, and allow for softer or slippery ground after rain or snow. With the interstate nearby, traffic sound is a reasonable planning consideration. Ask Technology Park about the current route and any access details your family needs. A separate note for the visitThe highway, the distance & elopement planning Yes—when you drive past the whale tails on I-89, you are on the interstate. That wonderfully unexpected highway glimpse was my sign that I was almost home. Technology Park places them between exits 12 and 13. To visit on foot, leave the highway and use the park’s trail approach. Do not stop on the interstate shoulder or try to walk in from I-89. How close is the highway? Roughly 100 feet (30 metres) from the sculptures to the nearest paved edge of northbound I-89. This is our straight-line estimate from 2024 Vermont aerial imagery, checked for this story—not a surveyed distance, a walking route or a safety buffer. It is also entirely separate from the distance you walk from parking. For a family planning around elopement or wandering, that proximity deserves attention. The CDC describes wandering as leaving a safe area or responsible caregiver, and identifies traffic as a danger. It can happen even with attentive supervision. This is a planning consideration, not a report of an incident on our visit. Boundary fencing appears in reference photographs, but we have not verified its present condition or a continuous barrier around the walking area. Treat this as an outdoor trail beside a highway, rather than an enclosed play space. Plan the close support your child needs before leaving the car, agree who is staying with them during photographs, keep familiar communication supports available, and make room for “break” or “all done.” The photograph can wait. If the setting does not suit your family that day, the passing view from a safely driven car can be the whole experience. There is no need to turn an old sign of home into an outing that asks too much. More views & useful reading For more photographs, see Jim Sardonis’s official Reverence gallery and Trail Finder’s photographs and trail map, including a winter view. The photograph of James above is from our family collection. Technology Park: The Story of the Whales Tails — location, dimensions and history. Trail Finder: Whales Tails Walking Path — route, surfaces, fee listing and trailhead. CDC: Wandering (Elopement) — general planning information. Sometimes, all you need is a really good cookie. Cookie Monstah in Burlington, Massachusetts, is one of those happy little stops our family loves. And if these pictures of James tell you anything, it's that a cookie can also be a fashion accessory. On this visit, James settled into a seat with his iPad nearby, held up his colorful cookie, and treated us to a series of expressions that were every bit as delightful as the treat itself. That mischievous grin is one of my favorite things in the world. One of the things I've come to appreciate about our family outings is that the smallest moments often turn into the best memories. An ordinary stop for something sweet becomes an opportunity to sit together, enjoy a familiar favorite, and simply be. One more expression for the family album. Cookie Monstah, Burlington. For families like ours, having time and space to enjoy an outing at our own pace makes a difference. We appreciated being able to sit down during this visit rather than turning our cookie stop into another hurried errand. Cookie Monstah has earned a spot in our family's little black book of places we love returning to. title: Disabled parking: the practical family guide.
summary: Handicapped parking permits, nonvisible disabilities, passenger use and safer arrivals: a family guide with official links for MA, RI, NH, Maine and Vermont.
search: Caregiver tools · Access starts at arrivalDisabled parking: the practical family guide.A small placard. A more manageable arrival. Where to begin, what to ask, and the official forms for five New England states.October 16, 2026 · A researched family guideOriginal editorial illustration. Display a placard while parked; remove it before driving. Some outings begin before we reach the door. There is the car, the traffic, the distance across the lot, and the person beside us who needs support for that part of the day. A disability parking placard—often called a handicapped parking pass—can be a useful access tool for someone who qualifies. A shorter route or room to use mobility equipment can make an arrival more manageable. The need is not always obvious to a stranger looking across a parking lot. This guide gathers the official starting points for five New England states. Start with the state where the person lives, and take the current form to the clinician who understands their needs. Who can qualify? A wheelchair is not the only reason someone may qualify. State criteria can include specific walking limitations, certain heart or lung conditions, blindness, or qualifying neurological conditions. The details differ by state. A diagnosis by itself does not guarantee a placard. Autism, epilepsy, a nonvisible disability or a history of elopement should not be presented as automatic eligibility. Ask the clinician to explain the person's actual limitations and support needs against the state's criteria. The motor-vehicle agency decides the application. For example, Massachusetts lists specific eligibility conditions, including being unable to walk 200 feet without resting or needing another person's assistance to walk. Its application asks the clinician for a qualifying clinical diagnosis and supporting information. The person does not have to be the driver. A qualifying passenger, including a child, can have a placard. Apply in the name of the person with the disability, following the state's parent or guardian instructions. A placard belongs to that person; it is not a general parking privilege for the household. New Hampshire's application, for example, explains that a placard can travel with its holder in different vehicles and that the holder must be getting out when the vehicle uses an accessible space. Check the rules wherever you park, including local meter rules. When elopement is part of the picture For a person who qualifies, reducing the journey through a busy parking area may help the family manage an arrival. But a closer space does not guarantee a safe route, and a placard does not prevent elopement or replace supervision. Before opening the door, agree which adult is supporting the person and where you are going. Look at the actual path: moving cars, crossings and the entrance matter as much as distance. Keep familiar communication supports available, and use the person's established safety plan. For dedicated wandering-prevention and response planning, see the National Autism Association's free Be REDy booklets and AWAARE resources. Those are useful companions to a conversation with the person's care team. Find your state's application These links lead to official agencies and forms. Use their current instructions for eligibility, certification, submission and renewal. MassachusettsComplete the RMV application with the required healthcare-provider certification. Placards have no application fee. The RMV asks for the original completed application by mail and recommends keeping a copy; allow at least 30 business days for processing.RMV application instructions and current form → Rhode IslandThe DMV's disability-placard application requires physician certification. Temporary, long-term and permanent placards have different validity periods. Use the DMV's disability page and current new/renewal form for the appropriate application route.Rhode Island placards and application links → New HampshireNew Hampshire calls this Walking Disability Privileges. Form RDMV 130 includes the application, medical-certification section and practical questions about passenger use and renewals. The instructions describe applying by mail or at a DMV location.Official RDMV 130 application and instructions (PDF) → MaineMaine uses form PS-18 for disability plates and placards. The BMV explains qualifying limitations, medical certification, temporary and permanent credentials, and proper display. Its page also links the application.Maine BMV guide and application → VermontFor a permanent placard, begin with VD-120 and review the medical-report requirement, VS-113. Vermont provides a separate temporary-placard form. For a minor, the permanent application instructs families to use the child's name.Vermont placard information and forms → Connecticut and other statesUse the federal government's directory to find your state's motor-vehicle agency and its disability-parking application. Requirements from a neighboring state are not a substitute for your own state's rules.Find your official state motor-vehicle agency → A small checklist before applying Open the current official form and read the eligibility criteria. Describe the person's actual walking limitations and required assistance to their clinician, including safety concerns where relevant. Check both applicant and clinician sections for required signatures and dates. Keep a copy and submit it within the state's stated deadline. After approval, note the expiry date and read the display and use rules. Once the placard arrives Use it only for the person to whom it was issued. Display it as directed while parked and remove it from the mirror before driving. Keep the striped access aisle clear—it is space people need to enter and leave vehicles, not an extra parking space. If accessible spaces are occupied, ask the venue about an appropriate drop-off or another practical entrance. Keep the plan flexible. The point is to make room for the day you came to have. Official application pages and published instructions checked October 16, 2026. This is general family-planning information, not an eligibility determination or individualized medical or legal advice. Agencies can change forms and requirements; the current official instructions control. Explore related topicsThe journal / Family & caregiver tools Advocacy & inclusion

title: Wandering is the activity.
summary: Inside the Book Barn in Niantic, Connecticut: room to wander, browse and take your time, with real outing observations and useful visit notes.
search: The Book Barn, Niantic · from our family camera roll.The Book Barn · a family field noteWandering is the activity.Books, gardens and curious corners. An afternoon without a prescribed route. Come alongA bookstore with room around it.The Book Barn feels like someone forgot to put walls around a bookstore. Books outside, books inside, gardens and odd corners. Our plan leaves space for wandering and one promising shelf.Looking for practical details? From our family notebook · NianticA bookstore without a script.The Book Barn is technically a used bookstore, but that description is as incomplete as calling the Maine coast “some water.” It is books, yes, but also paths, porches, garden corners, little buildings, signs, animals and the gentle feeling that the rules of an ordinary shop have loosened their tie.That is what we love about it. You do not enter and immediately feel the pressure of a proper cultural outing. There is no single route through the experience, no exhibit you are supposed to appreciate in the correct order. Someone can browse mysteries. Someone else can stay outside. You can look at three shelves or thirty. The wandering is the activity.From the existing family notebook. The photograph is our own; the decorative illustrations are interpretations, not current venue photographs.A subject that catches your eye is a good place to begin.From the rest of our notebook +On our visit, the place felt almost designed for a family that does better when the day contains choices but not demands. We could move. We could separate and come back together. We could notice whatever caught our attention instead of trying to maintain one shared pace. The atmosphere did much of the work for us: old books, greenery, bits of shade, curious corners, that slightly eccentric New England conviction that a perfectly reasonable business can sprawl across a property like a village.It is also the sort of place that gives a camera roll some texture: not a row of posed smiles, but hands on book spines, a path disappearing around a corner, a funny sign, someone absorbed in something that caught their eye. Those are the photographs we tend to keep. They look like the day felt—interesting, a little untidy, and entirely our own. Books and animals belong to the story. This cat is an illustration.The find is part of itOne promising shelf.And used bookstores have another advantage: they make very small victories feel satisfying. You do not need a major purchase. Finding one strange title, one old cookbook, one book about a topic somebody loves—that is enough. The object becomes a souvenir without announcing itself as one.Browse. Wander. Step outside. Leave when you are ready.What stays with us is the feeling of permission. Browse. Wander. Step outside. Look at something else. Come back. Leave when you are ready. It is a place with texture rather than a schedule, and that makes it one of those rare stops where the grown-ups can genuinely enjoy themselves without needing everybody to enjoy it in exactly the same way.Family story retained from our earlier notes, memory and camera roll. title: Before you go.
summary: Practical notes to copy and adapt before an outing, school meeting or everyday plan. Clear questions, useful wording and details worth checking.

Plan a day out Seven questions before you go A little more information before leaving the house can save a lot of guessing when you get there. When is it quieter?Ask about crowds, music, hand dryers, and scheduled events. Where can we take a break?Check for a calm space and whether you can leave and re-enter. What are the bathrooms like?Ask about privacy, space, and the specific facilities you need. What can we bring?Confirm food, drinks, communication devices, and familiar comfort items. How does the visit actually work?Check queues, parking distance, steps, seating, and any required waiting. Is the main attraction open?Confirm today's availability, hours, age rules, and access restrictions. What happens if plans change?Ask about cancellation, refunds, and a shorter visit before booking. ShareCopyPrint Ask for access A clear request can be short. Explain what gets in the way, say what would help, and ask for a reply in writing. A note you can borrow Hi, we're planning to visit [place] on [date]. A family member has a disability, and [barrier] makes it difficult to take part. Would it be possible to [specific adjustment]? Please let us know what you can arrange and who to ask for when we arrive. If that won't work, is there another option? A written reply would help us plan. Thank you! Copy this request Be specificCould we wait somewhere quieter until it's our turn?Could you send a few photos or tell us what happens during the visit?Can our support person stay with us?Could we have the instructions in writing too? You can begin with the access need. Your family's entire history needn't go into the first email. US guidance: businesses open to the public and effective communication. Duties and exceptions depend on the setting. This is a starting point for a request, not individual legal advice. Hotels and pools A lovely lobby is a bonus. A working pool and the right beds are rather more important. The room: what are the actual beds? Does the separate sleeping area have a door? “Suite” leaves a surprising amount unanswered.The pool: is it open on your dates? And the hot tub? Ask about hours, age rules, and water temperature if it matters to you.The timing: can you swim before check-in or after checkout?The food: what exactly is in the kitchenette? A fridge and microwave won't do the same job as a stove.The noise: ask about events, room location, and somewhere to take a quiet break.The bill: get the total with taxes, parking, fees, and deposits. Read the cancellation terms before paying. Hi, we're looking at a stay on [dates]. Could you confirm the beds and room layout, what's in the kitchenette, and whether both the indoor pool and hot tub will be open? We'd also like their hours and age rules, and whether we can use them before check-in or after checkout. Please include the total with mandatory fees, any deposit, and the cancellation terms. We also need [access adjustment]. Thanks so much! Copy the hotel questions Ask the property about your actual dates. An old pool photograph can only tell you so much. Support communication Please speak to the person. Give them time to answer. Those two things are a very good place to start. AAC means augmentative and alternative communication. Speech, vocalizations, gestures, signs, photographs, objects, writing, spelling, eye gaze, switches, low-tech boards and speech-generating devices can all be part of one multimodal system. Keep the person's communication method within reach. Ask before moving or touching a device.Leave time for a response before asking the question again.Offer choices the person can use, including “no,” “stop,” and “break.”Use language that respects their age. Speech alone doesn't tell you what someone understands. A note for a hostPlease speak directly to our family member and give them time to respond. They communicate using [method]. Please keep it available and ask before touching their device. It helps to [individual preference]. They may also need time to pause. Thank you for making room for this. Copy the communication note Read the full multimodal communication guide → Further reading: CommunicationFIRST, its guidance written by AAC users, and ASAN on autism. Understand ableism Ableism can show up in an ordinary exchange: talking over someone, dismissing an access request, or assuming a person won't enjoy an activity because they need help with it. Some autistic people need substantial support throughout their lives. They still have preferences, privacy, and every reason to be included. What that means hereInclude the person in the conversation.Speak to them, with the communication support they use.Allow a different sort of visit.A break, a shorter stay, or watching before joining in can make the day work.Keep support available.Comfort and communication shouldn't have to be earned.Let private moments stay private.A hard day doesn't need to become a public story. We write as a family. Autistic people speak for themselves, including through AAC, and their own words matter. ASAN on autism · CommunicationFIRST's wording guide If an access request is refused Ask for the reason in writing. It gives you something specific to respond to. Restate the barrier and the adjustment you asked for.Ask which policy applies, and whether another arrangement would work.Find out who can review the decision.Keep the dates and messages. Write down what happened while it's fresh. Thank you for getting back to us. The difficulty is [barrier], and we asked for [adjustment]. Could you explain why that isn't possible, share the relevant policy, and let us know whether an alternative would work? Who could review the request? We'd appreciate a written reply. Copy the follow-up For US rights guidance: businesses, government programs, and Massachusetts communication access. The rules depend on the setting; a refusal alone doesn't establish a legal violation. Make the day simpler One good thing is plentyPick the part of the day everyone is looking forward to. Leave space around it, and know what the shorter version looks like. Before the shoes go onConfirm the hours, parking, bathrooms, and food.Show what comes first, next, and afterward in a familiar way. Actual photos can help.Know where you can take a break, and how to get back to the car. For the bagA communication device and charger, familiar food and drink, a comfort item, spare clothes if needed, and the supplies in the person's usual support plan.There is no prize for staying longer than everyone wants to. Choices, routines & things to do Today's choices, pleaseA choice board needs to match what's actually available. For an ice-cream stop, that means today's flavors at the right shop.Offer a few clear choices, with words and useful pictures.Keep flavor, cone or cup, and size as separate decisions.A strawberry picture says more than a pink square.Include “something else,” “no,” and “finished.” Allow time to choose. If plans change: [how to explain or contact us]. Please follow the existing support and emergency plans.Copy the handover note Share private care details securely with the people who need them. More on communication support. Clothes that feel right A beautiful sweater that nobody wants to wear is still a sweater sitting in a drawer.Start with the clothes that feel right. One brand's medium isn't every brand's medium.Check washing and drying before buying.Build around a comfortable shape or color that already gets worn.Read the return policy, especially when ordering an unfamiliar fabric.Classic can be quite simple. Comfortable clothes, a useful layer, and no argument with the waistband.Build a useful wardrobe One family. Not the whole spectrum.We write about what we wear, where we go, what earns space in the house, and the practical side of life with profound autism. The point is not perfection. It is knowing enough to make a better choice before spending the money or loading the car.Our family experience includes profound autism and very high support needs. We do not use it as a hierarchy of human worth.When we write generally, we usually use identity-first language such as autistic person, while respecting individual preferences when they are known. title: Halloween, farm style.
summary: Skeleton glasses, corn sifting, a farm ride and memories of Connor’s Halloween Party at Frerichs Farm in Warren, Rhode Island.
search: The journalWarren, Rhode IslandA Halloween family field note Skeleton glasses. Cookie in hand. Not a bad way to start a Halloween story.A family afternoon at Frerichs FarmHalloween, farm style.A cookie, some spectacular skeleton glasses, corn to sift—and a farm that made a special Halloween invitation to autistic families.An AUsome Life · Published October 7, 2026 From an earlier family visitSome photographs bring back a whole afternoon. These are the ones with a yellow Black Panther shirt, a bit of Halloween mischief, and the three of us sitting close together in the October sunshine.They were taken at Frerichs Farm in Warren, Rhode Island. They still make me smile. Opened from the family albumA little skeleton and a lot of personality.The Halloween glasses deserve their own place in the album. White plastic bones frame a tiny skull, held up in front of one eye. A cookie is being kept very firmly in the other hand. The shirt is bright yellow, and absolutely none of the photograph looks like it needed organizing by an adult.Behind him, people are sitting under a big tent. The grass is green, the light is lovely, and it is the kind of unplanned photograph that ends up meaning more than the ones we spend ten minutes trying to pose.For us, these little moments are the story. Not how many attractions we did, or how much we fitted into an afternoon. Just the part we actually enjoyed. Pour, sift, watch, repeat. A good activity does not have to hurry.All three of us together in the autumn sun. A small activity, a real memoryThere was a table full of sand and corn.The sifting station was a wonderfully simple thing: a shallow tabletop, scattered corn kernels, a wooden screen, and a paper cup for pouring. It offered something to do with your hands and something interesting to watch happen.I love that we kept a picture of it. Sometimes the most absorbing stop of the day is not the grand attraction. It is an ordinary little activity that makes sense immediately, with no instructions required. A small study in autumn. Original editorial illustration.The invitation that matteredConnor’s Halloween Party.Frerichs Farm has hosted a special gathering called Connor’s Halloween Party, created for people on the autism spectrum and their families. It has been offered free of charge, with an RSVP, as a chance for families to enjoy some autumn fun together.That intention is part of why I wanted this farm in our family journal. A place can have pumpkins, wagons, treats and games, but there is something extra meaningful about an event that deliberately says to families like ours: this day is for you, too.Previous descriptions of the party mention activities such as the Western Town, pirate ship, bubbles, a scavenger hunt, a bouncy house and food. Activities can change by year, and a designated autism event is not a guarantee that every sound, surface or crowd will suit every person. title: A grocery run, then breakfast by the water.
summary: A Saturday Hannaford stop during our off-season trip to Wells, Maine: Oakhurst eggnog cold brew, our own plates and glasses, and breakfast at a waterside picnic table.
search: Hannaford · Our off-season Wells tripA grocery run, then breakfast by the water.Oakhurst eggnog cold brew, our own plates and glasses, and a waterside picnic table. A simple Saturday breakfast idea from our Maine getaway, with a grocery stop James was very happy to make.October 18, 2026 · From the family notebook The makings of breakfast on our Wells trip, before we found our table by the water. On our trip to Wells, a quick Saturday morning stop at Hannaford became breakfast at a picnic table by the water. We had brought our own glasses and plates, so our grocery-store breakfast got a proper little table setting. I’ve loved Hannaford for years. I lived in Vermont for a long time, and it is one of those familiar places I’m always pleased to see when we’re away. I was hoping for my favorite butter rum muffins. They were sold out, which was a small disappointment, but we found plenty else to enjoy. We picked up assorted muffins, chocolate-frosted donuts, cold brew and Oakhurst eggnog. The eggnog added a Maine connection of its own: Oakhurst is a longtime Portland dairy. At our waterside table, we mixed eggnog into the cold brew and made our own eggnog coffee drinks. James had his eggnog on its own. It’s never off-season for eggnog. James had a good morning in the aisles, too. James loves grocery shopping. He was enjoying himself so much that other shoppers commented, and we proudly shared that he is often the grocery-store trip leader in his classroom. Shopping is one of his favorite things to do, and it was lovely to have a chance to tell people about that part of his school day. Then it was breakfast by the water: muffins, donuts, our little cold-brew experiment and time to sit together. We enjoyed it so much that we forgot to take a waterfront photo. The butter rum muffins can stay on the list for next time. Original editorial illustration, inspired by breakfast during our off-season Wells trip. A small idea to borrowBring the table setting. title: A date at the Gardner.
summary: A date at Boston’s Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum, with our own photograph, practical caregiver planning, admission savings and museum accessibility notes.
search: Boston, Massachusetts · Time for two A date at the Gardner. A beautiful place, a little time together, and a photograph of just the two of us. There is room for this part of family life, too. October 16, 2026 · From our family album Just the two of us at the Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum in Boston. There is a place in our family album for just the two of us. Here we are at the Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum, tucked beside a stone column, with that extraordinary courtyard behind us. A little Boston date, worth keeping. So much of family life happens in conversation about what needs doing next. The calendar, the ride, the groceries, the things that need remembering. I like having a photograph that holds something else: us, together, somewhere beautiful. The Gardner makes a lovely setting for that sort of outing. The courtyard gives you something to pause over before you have made a single decision about which room to see. Its plant displays change through the seasons; the museum’s own courtyard guide is a good place to see what might be there on a future visit. A museum date can be wonderfully modest. Choose a few rooms. Point out a detail you like. Ask which painting your partner would take home if such things were permitted. Leave enough time to enjoy being there without making the entire collection an assignment. Time together belongs in the family calendar. Make the date small enough to happen. For parents and caregivers, getting out together can take real arranging. Reliable help, money and a workable window of time all matter. When those pieces are available, a short date deserves a place in the plan. An hour or two can be a perfectly good beginning. Before booking, agree who is covering care, the return time, and how to reach you if needed. Put the essential information in one place; our caregiver handover guide can help. Build in the journey home so the last room does not become a race against the clock. Choose one main stop and let anything else be optional. The museum lists Café G for food and coffee; check its arrangements separately if you want to add it. Leaving after the museum is also a complete date. And if a museum visit is beyond this week’s budget or support arrangements, keep the idea of time together in a smaller form: a cup of tea after the house settles, a shared album, a few minutes talking about something you are both looking forward to. The people doing the caring belong in the picture, too. The practical details left inBefore your own Boston date. Tickets, timing & a less expensive dateThe museum is at 25 Evans Way, Boston. Advance timed tickets are recommended. Standard adult admission is currently $25; ages 17 and under enter free. It is closed Tuesdays. Check current hours and availability on the official visit page.Thursday evenings are free, 5–9 p.m. Registration opens Tuesday at 10 a.m., two days beforehand; walk-up admission is not guaranteed. Use the Free Thursday Nights page to book. Participating library passes offer $5 admission for up to four adults; you must reserve the pass and obtain timed tickets with its code. A free evening may be busy, so choose the timing that suits you. Mobility, seating & sensory considerationsThe museum reports elevators in both buildings and a Palace lift to bypass the two steps before its main elevator. Free loan wheelchairs, rollators and canes are limited and first come, first served. Historic rooms have varied flooring, narrow doorways and low lighting; some power chairs may not fit every doorway.Gallery benches are available, with fewer on the upper Palace floors. Public restrooms have accessible stalls. These are the museum’s published provisions; we have not tested each route or facility. For individual access questions, call 617-278-5156 and review the accessibility guide. Ask about a quieter visiting time if crowds or sound affect your plans. Arrival & parkingThe museum has no dedicated visitor parking lot. Its directions page lists nearby options, including discounted Simmons garage parking with museum validation. The access guide lists two designated accessible spaces and a ramped loading zone outside the museum, plus four accessible spaces on Tetlow Street. Allow time for the trip between parking and the entrance. Check the official directions and parking information before setting out. If you are planning a later visit with the familyThis photograph is from our couple’s outing. A family visit can have its own pace and plan. Preview the museum’s visitor guidelines, keep communication supports available, and ask staff about any essential items or accommodations before arriving. A short visit with a clear ending is a useful starting point. Visitor information checked October 16, 2026 against the museum’s pages linked above. Hours, offers and arrangements can change. The photograph is from our own visit; the planning suggestions are for a future outing. title: A Little Heat on Cape Cod: Dinner at Kohinoor
summary: A recommendation from a local artist led us to excellent Indian food in Mashpee—and a restaurant where our son was made to feel entirely welcome.
search: Kohinoor · Mashpee, MassachusettsA Little Heat on Cape Cod: Dinner at KohinoorA recommendation from a local artist led us to excellent Indian food in Mashpee—and a restaurant where our son was made to feel entirely welcome.By Michael, James’s dad · October 25, 2026James’s picture choice board ↓ James at Kohinoor in Mashpee. First things first: Kohinoor served us the best Indian food we’ve ever eaten. We love Indian food, we have eaten plenty of it, and we have opinions. This meal did nothing to make us less opinionated. We found the place through Laura DiMeo, the artist behind Perch Pottery in East Falmouth. We had reached out about visiting her studio, and she graciously welcomed our family for what became nearly two hours of conversation and a personal tour. Meeting an artist where she works is a pleasure in itself. Laura was also a delightful host. When the conversation turned to our fondness for Indian cuisine, she recommended Kohinoor Indian Restaurant & Bar in nearby Mashpee. We took her advice. Our order was entirely vegetarian: samosa chaat, aloo gobi, palak paneer, and garlic naan. We also happen to love heat. Serious heat. The kitchen had no difficulty accommodating us. The food The samosa chaat was an excellent introduction. Pieces of samosa mingled with chickpeas, onions, and tangy peppers; sweetness, bitterness, spice, and crunch kept turning up in different combinations. There was a lot going on, and every part of it seemed to belong there. Next came the aloo gobi. We ordered the potatoes and cauliflower very spicy, and the kitchen took us seriously. Very seriously. The impressive thing was how much flavor survived all that heat. Both vegetables were cooked perfectly and retained their individual textures. You could still taste the potatoes, the cauliflower, and the spices. The heat gave the whole thing considerable force without flattening everything beneath it. Making food hot is one thing. Making it this good at that level of heat takes some care. The palak paneer was equally convincing. Fresh-tasting spinach, soft paneer, and a rich, creamy sauce with enough heat to keep things interesting (yes, we ordered this one spicy, too). The creaminess and spice worked beautifully together. Nothing seemed to be compensating for anything else. And the garlic naan: fragrant, flavorful, crisp in places and gently chewy in others. An excellent companion to the curries, though it hardly needed their help. Not a single dish disappointed us. At the table with James Our teenage son, James, has significant support needs. He also likes going out with his family. We like finding places where all three of us can enjoy a meal without spending much of it explaining ourselves. My wife photographed the menu and used ChatGPT to make a choice board: eight options with pictures James could point to. He has his own opinions about dinner; the pictures give him another way to make them known. The choice board made for James from Kohinoor’s menu. The food pictures are AI-generated illustrations, not photographs of the restaurant’s dishes. Download James’s choice board (PNG)An independent picture resource based on the menu during our visit. Check current choices with your server, and keep familiar ways to say no, ask for help, or choose something else available.The staff were entirely comfortable with James. More than that, they seemed to get a kick out of him. Their warmth was easy and unforced, and they were attentive to the practical things. They brought his drinks in plastic cups with lids, a small but thoughtful detail that made the meal easier. When we requested a plastic spoon, one appeared almost immediately. None of this became an undertaking. The drinks arrived in cups that worked for him; we asked for a spoon and got one. That sort of straightforward attention goes a long way. As James’s dad, I am fairly alert to the difference between a restaurant tolerating our presence and actually enjoying having us there. Kohinoor gave us every reason to believe it was the latter. James was another guest, with a family and an appetite. No awkwardness required. The restaurant itself was immaculate: soft green walls, warm pendant lighting, floral accents, and comfortable booths. Even the small details—the patterned pots and white blooms—were worth a look. The service was impeccable throughout. A few of the small details: white blooms, patterned pots, and green walls. Worth the return trip I could recommend Kohinoor on the aloo gobi alone. The palak paneer, samosa chaat, and garlic naan make that recommendation considerably easier. So does a staff who made having dinner with our son feel as ordinary and enjoyable as it ought to. We went in hoping for a good Indian meal. We came out revising our list of favorites. Thank you, Laura, for the recommendation. And thank you, Kohinoor, for looking after us so well. We’ll be back. title: Words matter. So does context.

So does context.An AUsome Life uses clear, respectful language and avoids turning disability into either tragedy or inspiration content.Identity-first by defaultWe usually use “autistic person” rather than “person with autism,” while respecting an individual’s own preference when known.High-support / profoundWe use high-support language when it helps explain access needs. “Profound autism” may appear when discussing the specific high-support experience this publication covers; we do not present the term as universally preferred or as a hierarchy of human value.No pity framingSupport needs can be significant without making a disabled person a tragedy, lesson or campaign prop.Age-respectful alwaysTeenagers remain teenagers. We do not infantilize someone because their communication, learning or daily-living support needs are substantial.For brandsWe will not use cure/fixing language, staged distress, forced participation or intimate private details to make a story more emotional. title: A birthday for our Lilo & Stitch fan.
summary: A Lilo & Stitch birthday at the Children’s Museum of Greater Fall River: homemade decorations, family photographs, and a museum rental memory with party-planning links.
search: Fall River, Massachusetts · A birthday memoryA birthday for our Lilo & Stitch fan.We rented out the Children’s Museum of Greater Fall River for James’s birthday, made the decorations ourselves, and brought a little of his favorite world along.From our February 2019 family album · Published October 22, 2026The party table, ready for everyone. Oh, this birthday. Looking back at these photographs makes me so grateful all over again. James’s great love of Lilo & Stitch made the theme an easy decision. We rented out the Children’s Museum of Greater Fall River and gathered everyone together to celebrate him. At the time, Lilo & Stitch wasn’t nearly as popular a party theme, so I made the decorations myself. Pineapple cups, flowers, tropical leaves, and Stitch himself at the table. A little February escape, right in Fall River. A little tropical color for a February birthday.Stitch had a place at the party, of course. There was the party, and there was a whole museum to explore. I love having both kinds of photographs: the table before everyone arrived, when you could still see all the work that went into it, and the room with everyone gathered around it. The people who made the day special. What stays with me most is everyone who helped make it special. When you’re planning a celebration for your child, you hope they’ll feel happy, welcomed, and surrounded by people who love them. We’re still so grateful to everyone who showed up for James and celebrated with us—and, of course, to the museum staff for helping make it such a lovely day. Time to explore the museum, too.Another little moment from the family album. A birthday built around something he loved, with people who love him. That’s a memory I’ll always treasure. Thinking about a museum birthday?Start with what your child enjoys, then ask the venue about the details that would help your family: private use, a place to take a break, entrances and exits, and time to set up. Our party is a family memory from 2019; confirm today’s arrangements directly.The museum is at 441 North Main Street, Fall River, Massachusetts. Its official party page lists party options and what families should bring. Check its current food and decoration rules before buying supplies.Explore birthday-party options → Plan a museum visit → · 508-672-0033Official links checked October 22, 2026. search: For immediate releaseOctober 4, 2026 An AUsome Life Launches New England Lifestyle Website New England living with the practical details left in: family outings, useful products, classic style and profound autism advocacy. MASSACHUSETTS, October 4, 2026 — An AUsome Life, a Massachusetts-based New England family-life publication, today announced the launch of its website at anausomelife.com. Building on the family’s existing Instagram account, the site brings outings, travel, home, classic style and useful everyday products together with a perspective shaped by raising an autistic teen with very high support needs. The publication looks at what makes a good day possible: a warm hotel pool, a quieter place to pause, clothes that feel right, food that works for the family and enough information to decide whether an outing is worth the drive. Its New England sensibility makes room for both an elegant coastal visit and an ordinary grocery run. Readers can explore family field notes, favorite places, practical guides and planning tools. Coverage connects the appealing parts of a destination or product with the details that often determine whether it works in everyday life, including pacing, comfort, cleanup, cost and the option to leave early. Profound autism advocacy is part of that editorial foundation. An AUsome Life addresses significant support needs plainly while keeping the person’s age, preferences and dignity in view. Its approach to universal design asks how clearer information, easier routines and more usable places and products can help a wider range of people participate. The site welcomes readers looking for good New England places, practical purchases and a more manageable family day, including parents, caregivers, extended family and people who simply appreciate useful details. Personal experience remains identified as one family’s experience, with reported information and future editorial plans distinguished from completed visits and hands-on reviews. The publication’s editorial standards call for clear disclosure of gifted, hosted, paid and affiliate relationships. A product or stay does not purchase a positive verdict. Journalists, destinations and brands can find editorial information and contact details in the media kit. Visit anausomelife.com and follow @anausomelife on Instagram. It covers New England outings and travel, home, classic style, useful products and profound autism advocacy, with a focus on everyday participation and the practical details that help families make their own choices. title: The Beautiful Art of Letting Go
summary: Three pairs of bare feet, an October ocean, and a father learning when to take a step back. An afternoon at Menauhant Beach in Falmouth.
search: Falmouth, Massachusetts · October by the seaThe Beautiful Art of Letting GoThree pairs of bare feet, an October ocean, and a father learning when to take a step back.A reflection from James’s dad · October 25, 2026James, with a whole afternoon in front of him. My wife took off her shoes first. We had stopped at Menauhant Beach in Falmouth early on Sunday afternoon. It was October, and this was a detour, not a swimming expedition. Nevertheless, off came her shoes and socks, and into the ocean she went. James saw his mother in the water and followed. Before long, I had abandoned my own shoes and socks and joined them. The water was ice cold. Bracing, certainly. Invigorating, if you were feeling generous. It was also rather difficult to argue with the two people already enjoying it. Eventually, Dad took his shoes off, too.The part of the afternoon none of us had planned. A little room My first instinct was to follow James closely. Watch each step. Anticipate the next one. It is a familiar reflex when you have spent years attending to a child’s safety: you begin to move before you have quite decided whether you need to. This time, I stopped myself. I was still watching. But I hung back. James has worked extraordinarily hard on his spatial awareness and his understanding of physical safety. There are hours of effort behind the things I was watching him do: learning, repetition, trying again. I knew that work. I had been there for it. Now I needed to make a little room for what it had made possible. James needed the freedom to be a teenager. He danced in the water. He ran from the incoming waves. His unmistakable sounds of delight carried across the beach. He was choosing when to approach, when to retreat, and when to do the whole thing again. There was nothing for me to organize. He was thoroughly occupied with his own afternoon. There was nothing for me to organize.The sea had his attention. I found that more moving than I had expected. So much of being his father involves helping him find his way through the world. It is possible to become so accustomed to helping that you fail to notice the moment when your help can take a quieter form. I could be there and let this belong to him. And there was my wife She had waded farther out, shielding her eyes from the afternoon sun and looking toward the horizon. She looked absolutely beautiful. A moment of her own. I loved seeing her that way. She was enjoying the water, the sunlight, the simple pleasure of having followed an impulse. For a little while, she had something that belonged to her. Family life, especially with a child who has significant support needs, asks a great deal of your attention. Schedules, concerns, the next thing that needs doing. Even on a good day, some part of you is usually looking ahead. Here she was, looking out. And here was James, dancing with the tide. I stood back and watched the two people I love most in the world. The lovely impulse that started it all.The two people I love most. Before the shoes went back on There was no ceremony to mark any of this. No carefully arranged activity, no formal acknowledgment of the work that had brought James to this particular stretch of water. There was my son enjoying himself. There was my wife enjoying herself. And there was the unexpected pleasure of realizing that I could simply enjoy them. Letting go, even a little, asks you to trust the work your child has done. It also asks you to recognize that the moment is his. James did not need me to give his afternoon a meaning. He already knew what he wanted to do with it. My wife, meanwhile, had reminded me how much can begin with taking your shoes off. For a little while, there was nowhere else to be. Eventually, we would have to put them back on. The schedules and responsibilities would still be there. But for a little while, on a beach in Falmouth, I watched my son move forward and my wife stand in the sun. I was glad I had joined them. I was glad, too, that I had known when to stand back. Three pairs of bare feet. One ice-cold ocean. And a moment of freedom I won’t soon forget. From the camera rollA little of the afternoon, moving.Two quiet beach films. Press play when you’re ready; these web versions are silent. Open the shoreline videoAt his own pace · 49 secondsRead a description of this filmJames stands barefoot on the sand beside the water. Small waves wash up and recede as he moves along the shoreline. Sunlight glitters across the sea; a stone jetty stretches out farther along the beach. Open the waves videoThe water comes back again · 20 secondsRead a description of this filmSeen from the beach, James faces the sea with his trousers rolled above his bare feet. The sunlight catches the small waves in front of him as they come toward the sand and draw back. Photographs by both of usA few more moments to keep.Open the rest of the album · six photographsA little room, and his father still there.A teenager, an October afternoon, and the sea.Sunlight, salt water, and a little time.His own afternoon.At the edge of the water.A wave comes in. A wave goes out. A companion to the afternoonThe shore has a story, too.I studied geology during my freshman year at the University of Rhode Island, before transferring. A shoreline has more than one story: the people who have gathered there, and the water, weather, and sand that keep changing it.A little history, a little science, and the practical details for finding this stretch of Falmouth. 01Before our footprints: a short history The history of this coast reaches far beyond its summer hotels. The Mashpee Wampanoag Tribe describes a presence in present-day Massachusetts and eastern Rhode Island extending more than 12,000 years. Its history and culture resources are a place to begin with the people whose homeland this region remains. A hotel, six cottages, and a wharfIn 1874, seven jewelers from Attleboro and John Tobey of East Falmouth formed the Menauhant Land and Wharf Company to establish a summer cottage community. Between 1875 and 1880, they built a hotel, six cottages, and a 120-foot wharf near Central Avenue and Menauhant Road. The hotel accommodated 150 guests. There were tennis courts, a baseball field, horses, bowling, and Saturday-evening dancing to an orchestra. It burned on June 17, 1918. The neighborhood survived; Jewelers Avenue still recalls those early developers. These details come from Kathy Lanson and Leonard Miele’s “Resort Hotels of Falmouth,” published by the Woods Hole Historical Museum. A beach still being madeThe present shore has its own history of care. In 2007, the town acquired 1.9 acres at the western end of Menauhant with town funds, Community Preservation Act funds, and help from The 300 Committee. The land trust describes the added beachfront as both public shoreline and a source of sand that helps nourish Menauhant. Read about the Haddad Beachfront. The beach is not a fixed stage on which the years pass. Waves, winds, and tides continue to move its sand. There is something fitting about coming here to watch someone grow. 02Warm sunshine. Cold water. Why? “Ice cold” describes how it felt to us; we did not record a water temperature. The bright blue photographs do not tell you how the sea felt around our ankles. Water takes much more energy to heat and cool than land does. That gives the ocean a slower seasonal rhythm: it stores warmth and releases it gradually. An October afternoon can feel lovely in direct sunshine without bringing the water anywhere close to summer-swimming comfort. The U.S. Geological Survey explains this high heat capacity. There is another difference your feet notice immediately. Water removes heat from the body much faster than air at the same temperature. So a temperature that feels quite manageable on your face can feel startlingly cold around your ankles. Massachusetts’ cold-water guidance explains the contrast. Sunshine is not a water-safety test. The National Weather Service cautions that unexpectedly cold water can affect breathing and movement. Check local conditions, keep the supervision and support your family needs, and have dry layers ready. 03Find Menauhant: map & visiting notes Menauhant Beach · Menauhant Road · East Falmouth, Massachusetts. The beach faces Vineyard Sound, with an inlet connecting to Bournes Pond. Open Menauhant Beach in Google Maps The town distinguishes Menauhant East, listed as public-welcome parking in its seasonal guidance, from Menauhant West, listed for resident-sticker parking. Check the Falmouth Beach Department for current parking rules, fees, closures, and staffed hours before setting out. Summer listings do not establish October services. Access planning: the Beach Department lists reservable adapted beach wheelchairs during its service season. Confirm availability for your date, the best access point, restroom arrangements, and your own needs with the department at 508-548-8623. Our photographs show sand and an uneven waterline; this visit was not a full accessibility assessment. A note from the family: giving James room here meant watching while allowing him to lead his own moment. Keep the supervision and water-safety supports your family needs. For a simple shoreline stop: bring a towel, dry socks, a change of layers, and whatever communication supports your family uses. title: Omar’s Superpower: Making Room for Everyone
summary: A family meal at Omar’s Bistro in Lexington, Massachusetts: from-scratch food, exceptional neuroinclusive service, comics, games, and practical parking notes.
search: Lexington, Massachusetts · Food, comics & communityOmar’s Superpower: Making Room for EveryoneA from-scratch kitchen, a world of comics and games, and the most neuroinclusive service our family has ever experienced. A little Lexington love letter, with the parking details left in.October 21, 2026 · An AUsome LifeA very good meal, and a smile worth keeping. Lexington has a superhero. His name is Omar, and his superpower is bringing people together. There are plenty of superheroes on the shelves at Omar’s World of Comics. But the story I want to tell starts with the person whose name is on the door—and ends, for our family, with James smiling over a basket of fries. Right in downtown Lexington, Omar and his family have built a place to eat, play, browse, work, and spend time together. It feels as though a wonderful from-scratch kitchen has been magically dropped into the middle of a comic-book universe. Happily, you can get lunch there. Every superhero has an origin story Omar Masood loves superheroes. A 2022 Lexington Observer profile describes his much-loved Marvel encyclopedia and his habit of matching people with superhero identities. The reporter got Jean Grey. That detail makes me smile: Omar inviting someone into a world he knows and loves. Omar, who has Down syndrome, is a graduate of the LABBB special education collaborative at Lexington High School. He and his family established Omar’s World of Comics in 2018. Pixel Paradise, the upstairs gaming space, followed in 2021; the bistro opened in October 2022. The business employs people with disabilities and partners with LABBB to offer vocational learning opportunities. Omar and his family have created a place where those opportunities are part of the everyday business of running a shop and feeding a community. His parents, Mona and Sohail Masood, deserve a place in this origin story, too. The Observer’s reporting describes their investment in a larger home for the business and the renovations that made its expansion possible. Omar’s sister, Laila, brought her love of gaming to Pixel Paradise. As a parent, I keep thinking about that: taking your child’s interests seriously enough to help build something around them, then opening it to the wider community. Their family’s work has given other families a place to gather. Headquarters has a very good kitchen Let’s give the food its due. Omar’s is affordable for our family, and that makes it somewhere we can return to for an ordinary meal. The fries are wonderful. The hot sauce is amazing. And the poutine deserves a little fanfare of its own: available vegetarian or with meat, and, in our expert opinion, the best poutine this side of Montreal. We had our first dates in Montreal—a long story for another day—so we do bring some relevant experience to this particular judgment. That is a fairly compelling reason to find yourself on Waltham Street. The kitchen’s from-scratch approach goes well beyond a nice phrase on a menu. Lexington’s visitor coverage describes daily bun baking, a house-ground burger blend, and spices toasted and ground in-house. Other diners have noticed the food and welcome, too. Customer reviews collected by Restaurantji praise burgers, fries, vegetarian choices, friendly staff, and value. Those are individual experiences, but the enthusiasm feels familiar after our own meal. Our kind of family outing: good food and time together. The welcome we felt at our table For us, the most memorable part was the service: the most neuroinclusive service we have ever experienced. When your child has significant support needs, a meal out can come with a running assessment in the back of your mind. Is he comfortable? Is this working? How much explaining will we need to do? It takes something away from the pleasure of simply sitting down together. At Omar’s, we felt welcome. We could enjoy our food and each other’s company. James could be James. And that welcome included the other patrons, too. The people sharing the space helped make it feel comfortable to be there as a family. A place takes on the character of the people who gather in it; we loved the warmth of this one. I keep looking at these photographs because I love his smile. An ordinary meal is worth remembering when everyone gets to enjoy it. As his mother, I also notice who gets to be part of a place: the people working there, the owner, the customers. I want James to grow up seeing disabled people in all those roles. Omar and his family have made those possibilities visible, right here in our community. Lunch at Omar’s, from the family camera roll.One more for the family album. A world to come back to With comics, games, and somewhere to sit down for a meal, Omar’s feels like a paradise for kids of all ages—including those of us who have been grown-ups for some time. The official event calendar gives people plenty of reasons to return. October listings include Minecraft Club, Pokémon League, trading-card games, and board-game playtesting. Activities have their own ages, costs, registration requirements, and participation expectations; read the individual listing to find a good fit. The people who create the comics are part of this world, too. Omar’s hosts visiting comic writers, artists, and game designers for signings and other events. Its May 2026 program, for example, included artist George Deep on Free Comic Book Day. Check the current calendar for upcoming guests. Omar’s also displays local art by disabled artists, giving their work a place in the everyday life of the shop. There is art to look at alongside the comics to browse, games to play, and food to enjoy. Artists, readers, gamers, families, people coming in for lunch: there are so many ways to enter this community. A shared interest gives people something to talk about and a reason to return. Our own adventure was a meal together. That was plenty. Omar’s gave us an afternoon we enjoyed and a place we want to come back to. Before you head to headquarters Find it: Omar’s World of Comics, Pixel Paradise & Omar’s Bistro, 20 Waltham Street, Lexington, Massachusetts. Check the official website and event calendar for current details; shop, activity, and kitchen schedules may differ. Parking: If the accessible spaces out front are full, our suggestion is the nearby Waltham Street municipal lot, accessible from Waltham Street or Muzzey Street. Check the town’s parking information and posted signs. Choose the space and route that work for your family. Our experience: Affordable food for our family, poutine available vegetarian or with meat, amazing hot sauce, warm fellow patrons, and exceptionally neuroinclusive service during our visit. Specific access needs: Our meal was not a full access assessment. Ask the venue about any particular seating, step-free route, restroom, sound, or support requirements before going. A friendly restaurant visit and participation in a scheduled gaming event are different experiences. Bring your appetite. Leave time to look around. And if you meet Omar, you’ll meet the person whose love of superheroes helped give this little world its start. The future I hope James gets to share What moves me most is that a business built with disability and opportunity in mind has become a gathering place for the whole community. People come for a comic, a game, a signing, a plate of poutine. Disabled people are part of creating the place everyone enjoys. That is our dream for James: a future with people who know him, places where he is expected, and interests that connect him to others. A place for his contribution, with the support he needs. Friendship, pleasure, and a life in the middle of things. We cannot know exactly what that future will look like. But sitting at Omar’s, I could picture more of it. To me, that is what a true superhero does: helps make the world bigger for other people. Omar and his family have made a little more of the future we hope for visible, right here in Lexington. We’ll be back for another adventure. History, reviews & visitor sourcesVenue information checked October 21, 2026. title: A Little Camelot in Boston
summary: With Mom-Mom at Boston’s April 2026 Profound Autism Summit: Governor Healey’s moving caregiving speech, wonderful questions, music, practical resources, and the 2027 dates.
search: Boston, Massachusetts · April 2026A Little Camelot in BostonWith Mom-Mom at the Profound Autism Summit: wonderful questions, music, a few tears, and a rare world arranged around helping us care for the people we love.An AUsome Life · A reflection on April 16–17, 2026A moment of connection at the April 2026 Profound Autism Summit. Some rooms ask you to begin with an explanation. Before you can ask your question, you have to explain your child. What support looks like in your family. Why an apparently simple suggestion might be complicated. How much you love someone whose needs do not fit neatly into the systems around him. At the Profound Autism Summit in Boston this April, I felt the relief of entering a room where so much of that was already understood. I went with my mother: James’s grandmother, our beloved Mom-Mom. The April 16–17, 2026 gathering at the Hilton Boston Park Plaza brought together people working to improve life for autistic people with substantial, ongoing support needs. We arrived as a mother and a grandmother, with the person we both love at the center of our reasons for being there. And for a little while, the world seemed arranged around helping us care for him. A little Camelot Camelot is the word I keep coming back to. For those days, the annual summit offers a rare world where the questions that occupy so much of our lives belong on the main stage. Communication. Safety. Adulthood. The ordinary, enormous work of helping someone have a good day and imagining how to make a good life possible. The difficulties do not disappear when we walk into a conference. But there is something restorative about finding a place where understanding them is a shared undertaking. Where people have gathered to think carefully, exchange what they know, and ask what could be better. There is room to learn. There is also room to exhale. Having my mother there made that feeling more personal. James is my son and her grandson. We love him from different places in the same family, and here we were, learning together. There is comfort in hearing something useful beside a person who already knows who you are thinking about. For a little while, the world seemed arranged around helping us care for the people we love. It began with someone they loved Behind the organizations that made this gathering possible are families who wanted more for someone they loved. Liz Martineau founded Nashoba Learning Group in 2002, inspired by her son with profound autism. That beginning matters to me: a mother taking what she knew about her child’s needs and helping build something that could serve other families, too. The Profound Autism Alliance, founded in 2023, grew from the Ursitti family’s experience. Cofounders Judith and Amy Ursitti brought a mother’s and a sister’s love for Jack to that work. Jack is himself named a cofounder and the organization’s Chief Inspiration Officer. Nashoba Learning Group created the summit in collaboration with the Profound Autism Alliance. Their work gives that deeply personal love a wider reach: more people to learn from, more questions to ask, more families who might find help. I felt that connection sitting beside my mother. We had come because we love James. So much of what surrounded us had begun with that same impulse: love for a child, a sibling, a person whose future matters. A Norwegian connection, courtesy of a sweater Then there was a small, lovely moment that had nothing to do with a presentation slide. A fellow Norwegian found my mother and me because I was wearing one of my favorite sweaters—a Dale of Norway. I love that a sweater could do that. In the middle of a gathering organized around one kind of shared experience, it opened the door to another. A familiar pattern, a little recognition, and suddenly a room full of people felt more connected. That belongs in my memory of the summit, too. Alongside the important information were the human details: my mother beside me, the people we met, and the unexpected ways we found one another. The wonderful questions I loved the questions. A thoughtful question can hold so much knowledge: what someone has already tried, what they have noticed, what still does not make sense, and what they hope might be possible for a person they love or support. Listening to those wonderful questions was part of the education. They brought the conversation close to daily life, where an idea has to work for an actual person, in an actual family, on an ordinary afternoon. The questions I carry into a gathering like this are very practical. How can we make it easier for James to tell us what he wants? How can we support his love of water while taking safety seriously? What helps him participate, make choices, and enjoy more of the world? How do we plan for adulthood while continuing to notice the life he is living now? A room that welcomes detailed, complicated questions gives us somewhere to begin. People, music, and the pleasure of being together At least a few profoundly autistic people attended, too. Their presence mattered. I want gatherings about support to make room for the people receiving it—to be there, to take part, and to have their own experience of the day. And the Flutie performers were absolute superstars. Their performance was amazing, one of the joyful memories I brought home. The Doug Flutie, Jr. Foundation for Autism helps make space for autistic artists and performers; at the summit, we got to enjoy the music and the people making it. There was so much serious work to consider, and there was also room for pleasure. I loved that. A good life needs both the right support and things worth getting together for. Ideas with a place in everyday life The photographs I brought home remind me how much of the learning concerned the texture of an ordinary day. One slide celebrated diversity in communication. Others explored picture communication, communication buttons, and AAC—augmentative and alternative communication. For me, the point is deeply personal: making more room for James to express himself, and helping the people around him become better listeners. I want his preferences to shape his life. His yes matters. His no matters. The things that delight him matter. Support should give those things more room. A reminder from the summit: communication can take many forms, and individual preferences deserve respect. There were Swim Angelfish visual supports for swimming, too, and an Inclusive Fitness presentation connecting physical strength with everyday actions: standing up, navigating a curb, carrying something, reaching a shelf. I appreciated the attention to the small details that can make participation easier. Visual supports and access to swimming.Movement connected with everyday life. Slide: Inclusive Fitness. Another slide described a family AAC camp at Zeno Mountain Farm, with activities built around autistic participants’ interests. The list included dancing, movies, karaoke, sledding, and s’mores. Even in a photograph of a conference screen, there was the lovely outline of a life: people having things to look forward to, together. A family AAC camp, and a list full of things to look forward to. The Lurie Center for Autism booth was especially informative. I appreciated having a place to stop, learn, and find out more. Useful information is easier to carry home when there is someone there to help you make sense of it. The center’s website also offers links to family education and resources for continuing that learning. That is part of what I mean by a world designed to help us care. Care includes access to pleasure, friendship, movement, and belonging. It includes the opportunity to try something because it might be fun. Governor Healey, and a future worth planning for Governor Maura Healey’s speech about caregiving brought a tear—or more—to my eyes. Hearing her speak, with my mother beside me, I felt how much it means for the work of caring to be recognized. So much of it happens quietly: the planning, the learning, the trying again, the love running through an ordinary day. It was moving to hear caregiving receive that kind of public attention. For anyone who would like to hear her remarks, the Profound Autism Alliance’s Massachusetts page links to the governor’s summit speech. Just weeks earlier, on March 23, she had signed Executive Order No. 656, establishing a framework for a statewide strategy to support adults with profound autism. The order calls for coordination across state systems and an advisory council to help shape that work. The state’s announcement explains the March 23 action. For a family thinking about a child’s future, that attention matters. Our children grow up. Their lives continue to deserve planning, investment, understanding, and people prepared to support them well. An executive order is a beginning. Its promise will matter most in the everyday lives of the people it is intended to serve. Still, it was meaningful to be there with my mother, at a gathering where that future was being taken seriously. A date for our next little Camelot The 2027 Profound Autism Summit is scheduled for April 15–16 at the Hilton Boston Park Plaza. I am glad there is another gathering to look toward. For families considering it, the official summit page is the place to follow announcements and check current registration details. Ask the organizers about participation needs and any available financial assistance. Getting away to learn can take considerable arranging when you are a caregiver; that part of the planning matters, too. In the meantime, the 2026 program and recording information and ProfoundVillage offer ways to keep learning between gatherings. What I want to bring home For me, naming substantial support needs belongs alongside respecting the full person: their communication, preferences, relationships, rights, and capacity to keep learning. I want a future shaped with autistic people, including people who need extensive support to participate and be heard. I want caregivers to have help, and I want the people we care for to have as much say as possible in their own lives. Those hopes belong together. That is what I want to carry out of our little Camelot. The summit gives us a brief experience of a world where people have come prepared to help. Each year, it makes room for questions that can be difficult to find room for elsewhere. It allows families to imagine what more consistent understanding could feel like. I went with Mom-Mom, wearing a sweater that helped a fellow Norwegian find us. I came away with ideas, wonderful questions, photographs, music in my memory, and a few tears I was glad to have shed. Above all, I remember being among people who understood why we were there. And I keep thinking about how lovely it would be to make more of the world feel like that. A place where our loved ones belong, and where helping them live well is something we do together. Keep learningThe 2026 summit page links to its program and session recordings.
