title: A little lake time.
summary: Fall foliage, lakeside boats and a rainbow: a lovely Rangeley, Maine getaway from our family's photo album, with practical notes for planning a visit.
search: The journalRangeley, MaineA grandparents’ field note The rainbow rather stole the show. From the family camera roll, Rangeley, Maine. Fall in the western Maine mountainsA little lake time.The grandparents, some downtime in Rangeley, and a very good reason to stop looking at the clock.October 6, 2026Mom-Mom & Grandpa Steve (aka Grandma & Grandpa) got a little time away in Maine. The photographs have all the ingredients I love: fall color, boats at the dock, a dog by the water, and a sky doing something magnificent.Grandparents deserve a chapter like this, too. From their corner of the lakeA day with room around it.There is something especially lovely about seeing the grandparents get a bit of downtime. We have plenty of family stories with a destination, a departure time, and several people’s needs to fit into the day. This little Rangeley chapter gets to be about a pause.Look at that shoreline: the boats tucked along the docks, the hills turning gold and rust, the ducks gathered near the grass. In one photograph, dark clouds sit above the village and a rainbow lands almost neatly behind it. Maine has apparently decided to handle the decorations.I love the ordinary part just as much. A jacket, a dog on a lead, a few minutes by the water. The sort of scene you might walk past while trying to get somewhere else—and then realize it was the thing you wanted all along. A little company at the water’s edge. The ducks appear to have called a meeting. A lakeside pause. Original editorial illustration inspired by a Maine landscape, not a map of the visit.The good partLet the view be the outing.A beautiful place does not need a very ambitious plan. For a grandparent getaway—or anyone whose idea of a holiday includes sitting down—I like the thought of choosing one lovely place and leaving time to enjoy it.A lake view can be the whole afternoon.That is the feeling I want to keep from these photographs: a little breathing room, a little fall color, and the people we love getting a turn to enjoy both.A broad sky, a patch of sunshine, and plenty to look at. Check the route from parking to your chosen seat, viewpoint or restroom with the site operator. For a lakeside picnicRangeley Lake State Park. Maine lists day-use parking, restrooms and picnic tables as accessible; the picnic area as generally accessible; the beach as accessible with assistance; and the trails as not accessible. Ask staff which route best fits your needs.The published day-use season is May 1–October 15, 9 a.m. to sunset. Off-season facilities close and entry is on foot from outside the gate, which changes the outing considerably.Park information & current notices · Official access ratings In-season questions: 207-864-3858 For the view, with less walkingQuill Hill. The operator describes a four-mile dirt road to the summit, parking at the top and panoramic views. That makes it an option to investigate when a mountain hike is not the plan. Ask about the surface between parking and the viewpoint, seating, and restroom arrangements.The site’s seasonal notices vary between “through October” and “mid-October.” Confirm the gate is open before setting out; cars, motorcycles and ATVs also use the road.Quill Hill updates · Official directions For a gentle wander, if it suitsHatchery Brook Preserve. Look beyond “waterfront.”For a stay, ask for the actual route from the car to the room and the lake view. Check steps, slopes, firm surfaces, bathroom layout, bed height and a place to sit with a backrest. The grassy slope and shoreline rocks visible in these photos are a useful reminder that a lovely view and an easy route are separate questions. Plan for sound, light and weather.Open water can mean wind, glare and boat noise; a scenic overlook can bring engines and conversation. Ask when a place tends to be quieter, bring familiar sensory supports if useful, and choose a stop with an easy return to shelter. A photograph cannot tell us how quiet a place felt. Keep the water’s edge optional.Enjoying a lake need not involve a dock or a boat. Choose a stable place to sit back from the edge. If close supervision around water is part of your family’s routine, build that into the plan. For a boat outing, ask separately about boarding, transfers and suitable life jackets. Give the dog—and the ducks—space.Check pet rules for the specific property and outing. Keep your dog close on a lead, leave wildlife room, and watch the ducks without feeding them. A pet-friendly listing is also worth checking for room restrictions and fees before booking. Before you leaveThe small, sensible list.Choose one main stop and confirm its seasonal opening.Check parking, the walking or rolling surface, a seat and an open restroom.Bring a warm layer, rain protection, water and something familiar to eat.Save directions before setting out and keep the return plan simple.Leave enough room in the day to stay a little longer—or finish early. For this field note, I keep coming back to the rainbow. The grandparents got their lake time, and we got these photographs to enjoy. title: A little research, a short car ride.
summary: A surprise Shaker history day in Harvard, Massachusetts: a thoughtful, inexpensive family gift, local history, and the craftsmanship behind Shaker furniture.
search: Harvard, Massachusetts · From the family albumA little research, a short car ride.Michael’s surprise Shaker history day: a thoughtful gift close to home, with James along for the adventure.Published October 22, 2026A family moment at Harvard’s Shaker burial ground. A little research, a short car ride, and a day planned around something I love. Such a thoughtful gift. ❤️ Michael surprised me with a Shaker history day in Harvard, Massachusetts, with James along for the adventure. I grew up right nearby, and despite being a history buff, I’d somehow never taken the time to explore this part of our local history. Apparently, I needed someone to turn “we should do that someday” into an actual plan. 😂 Harvard was home to the first Shaker community in Massachusetts, with roots going back to Mother Ann Lee’s visit in 1781. The remaining buildings and burial ground are reminders of a community that once farmed, worked, and worshipped here. The National Park Service tells more of the village’s story. My mother, Mom-Mom, has always loved Shaker furniture. Growing up, we’d make special trips to furniture stores in Gardner and Lancaster to buy pieces. That love of simple, beautifully made furniture was part of my childhood, so this day had a lovely connection to those memories, too. And then there’s the furniture. Those simple wooden chairs, beautiful cupboards, and carefully made tables reflect the Shakers’ beliefs about simplicity, usefulness, and craftsmanship. Even the familiar ladder-back chairs have a story beyond their appearance: they were practical objects made with extraordinary care. The Metropolitan Museum of Art explores that connection between belief and design.Original editorial illustration · the simple beauty of Shaker chairs. I love learning about the everyday details of people’s lives—what they made, how they lived, and what mattered to them. Getting to explore those stories so close to where I grew up, with my own family, made the day especially meaningful. It cost very little. The gift was the thought, the research, and having someone else take care of the planning. When you spend so much time organizing family life and caregiving, that part feels especially good. Thank you, Michael, for remembering the history-loving part of me and making a day of it. ❤️ A little history close to homeFor the background and a map of the historic village, start with the Harvard Historical Society’s Shaker history guide. It connects the surviving buildings, burial ground, and Holy Hill with the larger story of the community.For your own thoughtful outing gift, choose a subject your person loves, research a few nearby stops, and take care of the plan. title: A little winter adventure, right outside our door.
summary: Facebook Marketplace snowshoes, ski poles from a local free group, and a winter memory with James right outside our home.
search: Right outside home · From the family albumA little winter adventure, right outside our door.Facebook Marketplace snowshoes, ski poles from a local free group, and a winter memory with James right outside our home.Published October 22, 2026 · Updated October 25, 2026Secondhand snowshoes, free-group ski poles, and snow on our doorstep. Facebook Marketplace snowshoes, ski poles from our local free group, fresh snow underfoot, and James beside me—we were ready for a spontaneous winter adventure before we even had to leave the front door. ❄️❤️ I love a secondhand find, especially when it gives us a chance to try something together without spending a fortune before we even know whether we’ll enjoy it. We had snow, we had the gear, and we didn’t have to pack the car. A pretty good start! The grin came before the first step. Michael was still bent over the bindings, getting a snowshoe settled around a boot, and James was already beaming. Purple mittens up, knitted hat on, snow collecting on his navy jacket. There is a photograph of him looking straight at me with that enormous smile. I am very glad I kept taking pictures. Getting the bindings ready. The grin was already there. The poles from the free group were propped in the snow nearby. The snowshoes had their next pair of feet in them. I like seeing secondhand things at work like this: someone else has finished with them, and here they are in the middle of our afternoon. Then the little sequence unfolds: a step, a turn toward Michael, a look back at the camera. The blue frames stand out against the white. Snow is falling through every photograph. You can almost lose the houses and trees in it, but there is no missing his face. Purple mittens, blue snowshoes, and that face.Looking back, still smiling. Room to try. Room to finish. With James, planning an activity also means thinking about how to make it understandable and give him ways to tell us what he needs. Picture cards—including familiar cards for families who use PECS—can be part of that preparation: snowshoes, coat, mittens, outside, then home. Something concrete to look at while we talk about what’s coming next. And communication matters throughout the adventure. “Help,” “break,” “finished,” and “more” deserve just as much room as the plan itself. I want us to make space for what James has to say, however he communicates it. Being right outside our home gives us a little breathing room, too. We can take our time getting used to something new, keep the outing short, or head back inside. There’s no admission fee to justify and no long drive home if it turns out to be a five-minute kind of adventure. As a parent and caregiver, I appreciate that. I want James to have opportunities to try things, and I want those opportunities to fit him. Sometimes that takes preparation, visual supports, and the flexibility to let the day unfold differently than I imagined. I love our bigger outings, but I want to remember these days just as clearly: a Facebook Marketplace find, the generosity of a local free group, and time outside with my boy. Looking through the rest of these pictures, I keep coming back to how close everything was: Michael beside James, the poles within reach, the door nearby. We had room to try something without having to commit the whole day to it. And now we have the small details to remember: purple mittens held up in the snow, a parent crouched over a binding, that last look back. I want these in the family album alongside the trips we planned for months. There is a lot of life to enjoy just beyond the front door. ❤️❄️ More from the family album · six photographsA turn toward Michael.One snowshoe up.A few steps into the snow.The view from a few steps behind.Blue frames against all that white.Good company, close to home. Some places become part of your family’s summer. Twisted in Provincetown is one of ours. The giant pizza slice out front, the neon glowing in the windows, the evening bustle along Commercial Street—and that smile. When family outings take planning, having a place already on your “we love it here” list is its own small pleasure. You get to build on happy memories, year after year. Twisted is woven into our Provincetown summers: a cheerful stop in a town we love, and one of those places that makes a return visit feel familiar before we’ve even walked through the door. title: A little self-care, courtesy of Mr. Las Vegas.
summary: A bucket-list evening seeing and meeting Wayne Newton at Flamingo Las Vegas, plus real-world questions about VIP tickets, seating, sensory needs and access.
search: The journal / Las Vegas field note Las Vegas, Nevada · A night for me A little self-care, courtesy of Mr. Las Vegas. Meeting Wayne Newton was a proper bucket-list wish. The music was wonderful. The man, somehow, was lovelier still. October 16, 2026 · Visited October 12 · Flamingo Las Vegas An intimate evening under the lights at the Flamingo · from our camera roll. Somewhere between the calendar, the work, and remembering what everybody else needs, I keep a little list of things I have always wanted to do. Seeing Wayne Newton in Las Vegas was on it. Meeting him? That was the dream at the very top. I was in town for work, and it would have been easy to let the evening dissolve into one more email and an early bedtime. Instead, I went to the Flamingo for Wayne: Up Close & Personal on October 12. A little self-care, in a beautifully old-fashioned Vegas sort of way. Bugsy’s Cabaret is the sort of room that makes a performance feel less like a stadium concert and more like an invitation. There were red curtains, a small band, a guitar, archival pictures, and a lifetime of stories to tell. Wayne didn’t need fireworks. He had something rather more interesting: an extraordinary history and the gift of making it personal. Music can keep company with you for decades. Certain voices, songs, and the places we associate with them become part of the furniture of a life. I wanted to be there, in the room, to hear the stories behind the songs and see the person whose music had meant so much to me. The point of the evening was not to escape my life. It was to remember that I have a life of my own within it, too. For me, self-care is not always a spa appointment or a perfectly quiet hour with a book. Sometimes it is admitting that a wish matters, making the reservation, getting dressed, and going. It can be a big, sparkly thing. It can also be wonderfully simple: a little time that belongs to you. The part I will keep foreverAnd then I met Wayne. The VIP experience meant that after the performance I actually got to meet him, not just applaud him from my seat. There is a souvenir photograph to prove it, although I hardly need the reminder.
